b.x: When is root canal treatment needed?

When decay or trauma reaches the pulp, which contains the tooth's nerves and blood vessels, the pulp becomes inflamed. Common symptoms are prolonged sensitivity to hot and cold, pain that starts on its own or gets worse at night, pain when biting, and swelling of the gum.
In some cases there are no symptoms at all; a lesion at the root tip is only noticed on an X-ray. This is why regular check-ups and, when needed, imaging are important.
How is the treatment carried out?
1. Examination and imaging
The diagnosis is made with clinical tests and a periapical X-ray. If the root anatomy is complex or the size of the lesion is unclear, a dental CT scan (CBCT) is taken.
2. Anesthesia and isolation
Local anesthesia is given. The tooth is isolated with a rubber dam to keep it separate from saliva and bacteria.
3. Cleaning and shaping
The canals are shaped with rotary instruments and rinsed with disinfectant solutions. The canal length is measured with an electronic apex locator.
4. Root canal filling
The cleaned canals are filled with a biocompatible filling material to seal them.
5. Restoration
The upper part of the tooth is strengthened with a composite restoration or, if a lot of tooth structure has been lost, with a crown.
How many visits does it take?
Treatment can be completed in one visit or in several visits. If the infection is widespread, medication is placed in the canal between visits and the tooth is closed with a temporary filling.
After treatment
There may be mild sensitivity when biting for a few days.
It is recommended not to chew hard food on that side until the permanent restoration is done.
Healing is monitored with follow-up X-rays taken at set intervals.

faq.q: Does root canal treatment hurt?
faq.a: Root canal treatment is done under local anesthesia. There may be mild sensitivity for a few days after the procedure; this varies from person to person and usually fades within a short time.

faq.q: How many visits does root canal treatment take?
faq.a: The duration can vary depending on the severity of the infection and the complexity of the canal. In simple cases, the treatment can be completed in a single visit.

faq.q: Can a tooth with a root canal treatment break?
faq.a: If a root-treated tooth has lost a lot of tooth structure, the risk of fracture increases. For this reason, these teeth are often strengthened with a crown or an extensive restoration.

b.x: Implant treatment is a procedure that aims to restore chewing function in place of missing teeth by using artificial titanium roots placed in the jawbone. At our clinic, we plan the angle and position of the implant in advance with §b3D tomography and digital planning§/b.
In the surgical stage, we follow an approach that aims to protect the tissue as much as possible.
Our Implant Treatment Solutions
Implant Treatment
Restoring chewing function in place of lost teeth with titanium roots placed in the jawbone.
Used for single or multiple missing teeth
Requires regular care and check-ups
Supports chewing function
Does not require reducing the neighboring teeth
Guided Implant Surgery (3D)
Placing the implant at an angle and position planned in advance with 3D tomography and digital planning, with the help of a surgical guide.
Planning based on tomography
Performed with a surgical guide
Nerve and vessel positions are evaluated beforehand
Suitability is determined at the examination
What Is a Dental Implant?

A dental implant is an artificial titanium tooth root placed in the position of a missing tooth. The implant is surgically placed in the jawbone and fuses with the bone (osseointegration), forming a solid foundation. Restorations such as a crown, bridge or denture are mounted on this foundation.
An implant is one of the options available for missing teeth. How long it can be used varies from person to person, depending on oral hygiene, regular check-ups and general health.
How Is Implant Treatment Performed?
Detailed Examination and Planning
The structure of the jawbone and the positions of nerves and vessels are analyzed with 3D CBCT tomography. The implant position is determined in advance with digital planning software.
Implant Placement Surgery
Under local anesthesia, a titanium implant is placed in the jawbone. The procedure usually takes 30-60 minutes.
Healing and Osseointegration
A period of 2-6 months is allowed for the implant to fuse with the bone. Regular check-ups are carried out during this time. A temporary denture can be used if needed.
Placement of the Restoration (Crown)
A custom-designed porcelain or zirconia crown is placed on the implant. The color and shape of the crown are planned to match the neighboring teeth.
About the Treatment Plan

The scope of implant treatment varies depending on the bone structure, any additional procedures that may be needed (bone graft, sinus lift, etc.) and the material of the restoration. Because every patient's situation is different, the treatment plan can only be determined after a detailed examination.
You can make an appointment for a personalized treatment plan.

faq.q: Does implant treatment hurt?
faq.a: Implant treatment is done under local anesthesia. There may be mild discomfort and swelling after the procedure; this can usually be controlled with the pain relievers your dentist recommends. The process varies from person to person.

faq.q: How long does implant treatment take?
faq.a: Implant treatment is usually completed in 2-6 months. In the first stage the implant is placed, and then it is left to fuse with the bone (osseointegration). This period can take 2-3 months in the lower jaw and 3-6 months in the upper jaw. Bone quality and the patient's general health can affect this time.

faq.q: Is there an age limit for implant treatment?
faq.a: There is no upper age limit for implant treatment. The lower age limit is generally around 18, because jaw growth needs to be complete. If your general health allows, implant treatment can also be done at an advanced age.

faq.q: When can I chew after implant treatment?
faq.a: For the first 24-48 hours after the implant is placed, you should eat soft foods. During the healing period (2-6 months), excessive load should not be placed on the implant area. After the restoration (crown) is placed, you can continue chewing following your dentist's recommendations. Detailed instructions will be given to you after the treatment.

faq.q: How long do implants last?
faq.a: With proper care and regular check-ups, implants can be used for many years; however, this varies from person to person and no exact lifespan can be given. Oral hygiene, smoking and general health are factors that affect how long an implant lasts.

b.x: Periodontology is the branch of dentistry that protects and treats the health of the gums and the tissues that support the teeth. §bHealthy gums§/b are important for supporting the teeth. Studies show a relationship between gum disease and some general health conditions, such as diabetes.
At our clinic, we provide gum treatments ranging from preventive gum care to surgical procedures. We evaluate your smile esthetics and gum health together.
Why Is Gum Health So Important?
Gum disease is common and, as it progresses, it can affect the tissues that support the teeth. This is why noticing it early is important:
§bSupporting tissues:§/b Advancing gum disease can cause teeth to become loose
§bDiabetes:§/b Gum check-ups are especially important for people with diabetes
§bPregnancy:§/b Gum tenderness and bleeding may increase during pregnancy
§bEsthetics:§/b The level of the gums also affects the appearance of the smile

faq.q: Does tartar cleaning damage the teeth?
faq.a: Professional tartar cleaning done with the right technique does not wear away tooth enamel. Removing tartar and plaque helps protect gum health. Short-term sensitivity may occur after the procedure.

faq.q: What are the symptoms of gum disease?
faq.a: Bleeding gums, swelling, redness, bad breath, receding gums, loose teeth and deepening gum pockets are symptoms of gum disease. If you notice any of these, it is recommended that you see your dentist.

faq.q: Does pink esthetics treatment hurt?
faq.a: Pink esthetics treatment is done under local anesthesia. There may be mild discomfort after the procedure; this is usually controlled with the pain relievers your dentist recommends. Healing varies from person to person.

faq.q: Can receding gums grow back?
faq.a: Receded gums do not grow back on their own. In suitable cases, gum graft procedures may aim to cover the exposed root surface. An early examination is important for evaluating the options.

faq.q: How often should I have my teeth cleaned?
faq.a: How often you need a cleaning varies from person to person; tartar buildup and gum condition are evaluated at regular check-ups. Your dentist will determine the cleaning frequency that is right for you.

b.x: Prosthetic dentistry is the process of restoring chewing function and esthetics in place of missing or damaged teeth with §bfixed or removable prostheses§/b. At our clinic, we prepare custom prostheses, also making use of digital impression and design technology.
From zirconia crowns to acrylic dentures, we decide together after the examination which option suits each patient's needs.

Fixed Prostheses

Stay fixed in the mouth

Digital Prosthetic Dentistry
At our clinic, we use digital impression systems and CAD/CAM technology when making prostheses:
§bDigital impression:§/b An impression can be taken with an intraoral scanner instead of an impression tray
§bDigital design:§/b The prosthesis is planned and prepared on a computer
§bFit check:§/b Fit and bite are checked at the try-in stage

faq.q: What is the difference between a zirconia crown and a porcelain crown?
faq.a: Zirconia crowns have no metal framework and are made of ceramic material; because they let light through, an appearance that matches the tooth color can be achieved. Porcelain-fused-to-metal crowns are made over a metal framework, and in some cases a gray shadow can be seen at the gum line.

faq.q: How durable is a zirconia crown?
faq.a: Zirconia is a durable material and can be used on both front and back teeth. How long a crown lasts varies from person to person depending on oral hygiene, teeth-clenching habits and regular check-ups; no exact duration can be given.

faq.q: Does wearing a denture affect speech?
faq.a: There may be an adjustment period in the first few days; how long it lasts varies from person to person. With regular use and practice, speech usually becomes easier; if the problem continues, the denture can be adjusted at a check-up.

faq.q: How often should I clean my denture?
faq.a: The denture should be taken out and cleaned every day, after every meal. At bedtime, the denture should be taken out and kept in a special denture-cleaning solution. This is important both for hygiene and to let the oral tissues rest.

faq.q: Are the neighboring teeth damaged for bridge treatment?
faq.a: To make a bridge, the neighboring teeth are reduced (prepared). For this reason, implant treatment is preferred when possible. However, if an implant is not suitable, a bridge is an option that can be used in place of the missing tooth.

b.x: Esthetic dentistry is a treatment approach that aims to improve the appearance of the teeth. At our clinic, with §bDigital Smile Design§/b we can review the planned look together before treatment, and with a §bMinimally Invasive Approach§/b we aim to preserve healthy tooth tissue as much as possible.
After the examination, we create a personalized treatment plan for each of our patients.
What Is Digital Smile Design?

Digital smile design is a method that gives an approximate preview of the planned smile by making a digital simulation on your photos before treatment; the actual result may differ from person to person. This helps clarify your expectations, and we determine the treatment plan together.
Your face shape, lip structure and gums are analyzed to create a natural and esthetic smile design made for you.

faq.q: What is the difference between porcelain veneers and composite veneers?
faq.a: Porcelain veneers are thin porcelain shells prepared in a laboratory and bonded to the tooth. Composite veneers are composite material applied directly to the tooth. Porcelain veneers are more resistant to staining and require a laboratory stage. Composite veneers are mostly completed in a single visit and can be repaired when needed. Which one is suitable is determined at the examination.

faq.q: Is teeth whitening permanent?
faq.a: Teeth whitening is not permanent; how long the effect lasts varies from person to person. Consuming things that cause staining, such as cigarettes, coffee and tea, shortens how long the whiteness lasts. The effect can be extended with regular dental care and periodic whitening sessions.

faq.q: How durable is a zirconia crown?
faq.a: How long zirconia crowns last varies from person to person depending on oral hygiene, teeth-clenching habits and regular check-ups; no exact duration can be given. It is metal-free and a durable material; it can be used on front and back teeth.

faq.q: How long does a smile design take?
faq.a: The duration of a smile design varies depending on the treatment applied. Composite bonding can be completed in a single visit, while porcelain veneers require 2-3 visits. A zirconia crown is completed over a period of 2-3 weeks. After a detailed examination, a treatment plan is created for you.

b.x: Clear aligner treatment is an orthodontic method used as an alternative to traditional braces. A series of §bclear, removable§/b aligners aims to move the teeth to the planned position. Thanks to §bdigital planning§/b, you can review the planned movements in advance and follow the treatment process step by step.
At our clinic, custom clear aligners are prepared with 3D digital scanning and simulation. Each aligner aims to move the teeth gradually.
Orthodontics with Clear Aligners
Clear Aligner Treatment
Correcting crowded teeth through digital planning, without braces, using a series of clear, removable aligners.
Treatment Process:
§bDigital scan:§/b A 3D digital model of your mouth is created
§bTreatment planning:§/b A simulation of your teeth's movement is made and the planned stages are shown
§bAligner production:§/b A set of clear aligners made for you is prepared
§bStart of treatment:§/b You switch to a new aligner every 1-2 weeks
§bRegular check-ups:§/b Progress is checked every 6-8 weeks
Digital Orthodontic Planning
In clear aligner treatment, planning is done digitally. The simulation is a planning tool; the actual result may differ from person to person. With the 3D digital simulation:
You can see the planned position of your teeth at every stage
You can review the targeted tooth alignment in advance
You get information about the estimated treatment time
You clarify your expectations

faq.q: Can clear aligner treatment be used at any age?
faq.a: Clear aligner treatment is generally used after adolescence and in adults. It is important that jaw growth is complete. There is no upper age limit; it can be used at any age in suitable cases.

faq.q: How many hours a day should I wear clear aligners?
faq.a: Clear aligners should be worn at least 20-22 hours a day. They are taken out only when eating and brushing your teeth. Regular use is important for the treatment to progress as planned.

faq.q: How long does clear aligner treatment take?
faq.a: The treatment time varies with the complexity of the case. It can take 6-12 months for mild crowding and 12-24 months for moderate and advanced cases. The estimated time is shared with you during digital planning.

faq.q: Is speech affected during clear aligner treatment?
faq.a: There may be a mild adjustment period in the first few days; how long it lasts varies from person to person. Because the aligners are thin, speech usually becomes comfortable again in a short time.

faq.q: Can clear aligners be used for every type of crowding?
faq.a: Clear aligner treatment is mostly preferred for mild and moderate crowding. In advanced cases or serious jaw discrepancies, traditional orthodontics may be more suitable. The appropriate treatment is recommended after a detailed examination.

b.x: Oral and maxillofacial surgery covers a wide range of procedures, from tooth extractions to complex surgical operations. At our clinic, following the principle of a §bMinimally Invasive Approach§/b, we aim to protect the tissue as much as possible during surgical procedures.
When needed, planning is done with 3D tomography and the procedures are carried out under local anesthesia. The appropriate method is determined after the examination.
What Is Minimally Invasive Surgery?
Minimally invasive surgery is a surgical approach that aims to interfere with the surrounding tissue as little as possible during the procedure. In this approach:
Incisions and bone removal are kept as limited as needed
The aim is to protect the surrounding tissues
Planning is done with imaging before the procedure
Aftercare instructions are given and healing is followed

faq.q: Does impacted wisdom tooth extraction hurt?
faq.a: Impacted wisdom tooth extraction is done under local anesthesia. There may be discomfort and swelling for a few days after the procedure; this is usually controlled with the pain relievers your dentist recommends and cold compresses. The process varies from person to person and with the position of the tooth.

faq.q: Do wisdom teeth always have to be removed?
faq.a: No, not every wisdom tooth needs to be removed. If the tooth has erupted properly, is functional and is not causing problems around it, it does not need to be removed. However, teeth that stay impacted, press on the neighboring tooth, or cause infection or cysts need to be removed.

faq.q: How long does it take to heal after a surgical tooth extraction?
faq.a: There may be swelling and mild discomfort for the first few days. If stitches were placed, they are usually removed at a check-up appointment around one week later. The healing time of the soft tissue and bone varies from person to person; your dentist will tell you when you can return to daily activities.

faq.q: What should I pay attention to after a tooth extraction?
faq.a: During the first 24 hours, do not touch the extraction site, do not eat hot food and do not rinse your mouth. For the first 3 days, prefer soft and lukewarm foods. Do not smoke and do not make sucking movements. If medication has been prescribed, use it according to your dentist's instructions.

svc.d: An approach suited to children's psychology for the treatment, trauma care and follow-up of baby and permanent teeth.

b.x: Pediatric dentistry is the branch of dentistry that protects and treats children's oral and dental health. At our clinic, we approach your children with a §bgentle and understanding approach§/b and aim to minimize fear of the dentist. With our philosophy of §bPreventive Dentistry§/b, we focus on preventing decay before it forms.

Positive dental experiences gained in childhood contribute to the development of healthy oral care habits. With our play-based treatment environment and an approach suited to children's psychology, we aim to make it easier for children to get used to the dentist.
Why Is Preventive Dentistry Important?
Preventive dentistry focuses on preventing cavities and gum disease rather than treating them. This approach helps reduce the likelihood of needing more extensive treatments.
Fluoride Application
Helps increase the resistance of tooth enamel to decay. The dentist determines how often it is applied.
Fissure Sealant
Helps reduce the risk of decay by sealing the deep grooves of the molars.
Regular Check-ups
Regular check-ups help problems be noticed early.
Education
Education for the child and parents on proper tooth brushing and eating habits.
Tips for Parents
Start brushing when the first tooth comes in
Limit sugary and acidic drinks
Do not give a bottle at bedtime, to avoid baby bottle tooth decay
Present the dentist visit as a positive experience
Bring your child to regular check-ups every 6 months

faq.q: When should I first take my child to the dentist?
faq.a: You should take your child to the dentist when the first tooth comes in, or by age 1 at the latest. Check-ups that start early help the child get used to the dentist and make it possible to diagnose potential problems early.

faq.q: Baby teeth will fall out anyway, is it necessary to treat them?
faq.a: Yes, treating baby teeth is very important. Baby teeth are critical for chewing, speech and lower jaw development. They also act as space holders for the permanent teeth coming in from below. Baby teeth lost early can cause crowding in the permanent teeth.

faq.q: Is fluoride application harmful?
faq.a: Topical (external) fluoride application helps increase the resistance of tooth enamel to decay. It is done at a dose suitable for the child's age and under the dentist's supervision; following the instructions given after the application is recommended.

faq.q: What is a fissure sealant and when should it be done?
faq.a: A fissure sealant is a protective application that seals the deep grooves on the chewing surface of the molars. It is usually applied after the permanent molars come in (around ages 6-7 and 11-13) and helps reduce the risk of decay. Its suitability is evaluated at the examination.

faq.q: My child is afraid of the dentist, what should I do?
faq.a: Prepare your child with positive language and never frighten them. Use phrases like 'We will count your teeth' instead of 'It won't hurt'. At our clinic, we aim to help children feel comfortable with an approach suited to children's psychology and a play-based treatment environment.

b.x: Bruxism is the unconscious clenching or grinding of the teeth and usually occurs during sleep. §bTeeth clenching and grinding§/b can, over time, lead to tooth wear and jaw joint complaints. At our clinic, we evaluate treatment options aimed at reducing the effects of bruxism.

A §bnight guard§/b and timely repair of worn teeth can help ease symptoms and protect the teeth. These are addressed together with lifestyle recommendations such as stress management and sleep habits.
Symptoms of Bruxism
If you experience one or more of the following symptoms, you may have bruxism:
Comprehensive Treatment Approach
Bruxism treatment should not only ease the symptoms but also address the underlying causes. At our clinic, we use a multi-sided approach:
1. Protective Treatment
Protecting the teeth from wear with a night guard
2. Repair
Repairing worn or broken teeth with fillings or crowns
3. Lifestyle Changes
Stress management, sleep hygiene, reducing caffeine and alcohol consumption
4. Regular Follow-up
Evaluating how well the treatment is working and making adjustments if needed

faq.q: What is bruxism and what causes it?
faq.a: Bruxism is the unconscious clenching or grinding of the teeth. It usually happens during sleep but can also be seen during the day. Stress, anxiety, sleep disorders, a misaligned bite and some medications can cause bruxism.

faq.q: How long should I use a night guard?
faq.a: A night guard should be used every night for as long as the bruxism continues. The guard protects the teeth but does not treat bruxism. Treating the underlying causes (stress, sleep disorders) is also important.

faq.q: What happens if bruxism is not treated?
faq.a: Bruxism that continues for a long time can be associated with problems such as tooth wear, fractures and cracks, jaw joint complaints and headaches. It is recommended to have an examination when symptoms are noticed.

20-yas-disi-cekilmeli-mi.title: Does Every Wisdom Tooth Need to Be Removed? A Scientific, Evidence-Based Guide
20-yas-disi-cekilmeli-mi.lead: Risk analysis with 3D tomography and informed decision-making.

b.x: "My wisdom teeth are coming in, I think I need to have them pulled." This is one of the sentences we hear most often in our clinic, usually said with some worry. Wisdom teeth are almost always known in society as §b"problem teeth that must be removed"§/b.

Our aim in this guide is not to give you a simple answer such as "all of them must be removed" or "none of them should be removed." Our aim is to explain which wisdom teeth really pose a risk, which ones can safely stay in the mouth, and how in our clinic we make this decision §bnot by "guessing" but with "3D digital planning"§/b.
Why Are Wisdom Teeth Generally Known as "Problematic"?
The "bad reputation" of these teeth has a scientific basis. Wisdom teeth are the last teeth to erupt in our mouths, and they usually try to come in between the ages of 17 and 25.

During the evolution of modern humans, our jaws have become smaller than those of our ancestors. This reduction has left too little room for the wisdom teeth, the third molars at the very back, to erupt.
Teeth That Cannot Find Room: 3 Scenarios
§bImpacted:§/b The tooth stays completely under the jawbone or gum and can never come out.
§bPartially Impacted:§/b Part of the tooth comes through, but part of it stays under the gum or bone. (This is a scenario that often leads to problems.)
§bAngled Eruption:§/b Instead of coming in straight (vertically), the tooth tries to come in sideways, toward the cheek, toward the tongue, or toward the neighboring tooth in front of it.
"Extraction May Be Needed": Which Wisdom Teeth Should Be Removed?

"Evidence-based" dentistry does not recommend removing a tooth just because "it might cause trouble." We remove a tooth §bif it is causing an active problem, or if it is scientifically predicted to be highly likely to cause one§/b.
1. Pericoronitis (The Most Common and Urgent Reason)
§bWhat it is:§/b An infection of the gum around a "partially impacted" tooth. Food gets trapped in this gum pocket, cannot be cleaned, and creates an ideal breeding area for bacteria.
§bSymptoms:§/b Severe pain, difficulty opening the mouth (trismus), swelling of the face, bad odor, and sometimes fever.
§bSolution:§/b The infection is treated first with antibiotics, and once the infection has cleared, removal of the tooth that caused the problem is usually recommended.
2. Pressure on the Neighboring Tooth and Decay (May Cause No Symptoms)
This is an important scenario that the patient does not notice but that we can see on an X-ray. The wisdom tooth presses horizontally or at an angle against the healthy second molar in front of it.
§bResult 1 (Decay):§/b Food constantly gets trapped between the two teeth. Not only the wisdom tooth but, more importantly, the second molar also decays at the contact surface.
§bResult 2 (Resorption):§/b The pressure from the wisdom tooth can cause the root of the tooth in front to "dissolve."
3. Cyst or Tumor Formation

The "follicle" around a completely impacted tooth can, over time, collect fluid and turn into a "cyst" (dentigerous cyst). These cysts grow silently, dissolve the jawbone from the inside, and in very advanced cases can set the stage for jaw fractures.
4. Orthodontic Reasons (Crowding)
In patients who have had or will have orthodontic treatment, removing the wisdom teeth may be strategically necessary to maintain the alignment achieved or to create room to move teeth backward.
"Extraction Is Not Needed": Which Wisdom Teeth Can Safely Stay?
In our clinic we avoid "unnecessary surgery." If your wisdom tooth fits one of the scenarios below, removal is generally not needed.
Scenario 1: Fully Erupted, Healthy and Functional
If your wisdom tooth:
Has erupted fully like the other teeth
Closes fully against the tooth opposite it (is in function)
Is in a good position and can be cleaned fully with a brush and floss
Has no decay or gum problem
§bDecision:§/b This tooth is a healthy and functional part of your mouth. It does not need to be removed. It is only monitored at routine check-ups.
Scenario 2: Completely Impacted and Without Symptoms (If There Is No Risk)
If your wisdom tooth:
Is impacted very deep in the jawbone
Has no contact with the tooth in front of it or with a nerve
Shows no sign of a cyst or infection around it
§bDecision:§/b The surgical operation to remove this tooth may be riskier than leaving it in place. In this case the tooth is "not removed" and is only "monitored" with yearly X-rays.
Our Decision Process in the Clinic: Evaluation with 3D Tomography
How do we decide whether your tooth is "risky" or "safe"? Traditional 2D (panoramic) X-rays may not provide enough information to make this decision in some cases.
In our clinic, in impacted tooth cases where it is considered necessary, we carry out the evaluation with §b3D Dental Tomography (CBCT)§/b.
Why 3D Tomography?

§bEvaluating the Relationship with the Nerve:§/b It shows in detail the relationship of the tooth root to the lower jaw nerve. This is important information for planning aimed at reducing the risk of "lip numbness."
§bDiagnosing Cysts:§/b It contributes in more detail than a 2D X-ray to the evaluation of cysts or pathological formations.
§bRoot Anatomy:§/b It shows in 3D how many roots the tooth has and how the root tips curve.
§bDamage to the Neighboring Tooth:§/b It helps to assess the extent of the damage done to the tooth in front.
§bResult:§/b 3D tomography helps the decision to be made on the basis of imaging findings.
Conclusion: The Decision Is Individual and Scientific

The "evidence-based" answer to the question "Does every wisdom tooth need to be removed?" is: §bNo, but every wisdom tooth should be examined, and when necessary a risk analysis should be done with methods such as 3D tomography.§/b
Some teeth may cause problems in the future, while others can stay in your mouth in a healthy way.

At our clinic in Lüleburgaz, with our "Minimally Invasive" surgical approach and our "Digital Planning" infrastructure, we aim to avoid surgical procedures that are not necessary. Our goal is to plan and carry out carefully the intervention that is required.

20-yas-disi-cekimi-sonrasi-bakim.title: Nutrition and Care After Impacted Wisdom Tooth Removal: The First 72 Hours
20-yas-disi-cekimi-sonrasi-bakim.lead: Managing swelling, controlling bleeding and preventing dry socket.

b.x: Your impacted wisdom tooth surgery is complete. This was an important and brave step for your oral health. You are probably still under the effect of the anesthesia right now, and you have many questions in mind: §b"Will my face swell?", "What can I eat?", "How do I heal quickly?"§/b
This guide has been prepared to explain, with a dentist's clarity, the steps you need to take during the most critical §b72 hours (3 days)§/b ahead of you.
The Basic Rule of Healing: Protecting the Blood Clot

After surgery, the §b"blood clot"§/b that forms in the extraction socket is the foundation of healing. This clot is not a simple pool of blood; it is a natural bandage that your body sends to the area, full of healing cells, proteins and growth factors.

The clot is a biological shield that protects the delicate bone and nerve endings underneath from the outside world (food, bacteria, air). All the rules for the first 72 hours serve a single purpose: §bnot to dislodge this clot.§/b
An Important Complication: What Is "Dry Socket" (Alveolitis)?
The complication our patients worry about most is a condition called "Dry Socket" (alveolitis).
What Is Dry Socket?
It is the premature loss or dissolving of the valuable blood clot we mentioned above, earlier than it should.
What Is the Result?

When the clot is lost, the jawbone and nerve endings underneath are directly exposed to the environment of the mouth. The result is a throbbing, §bsevere pain§/b that usually begins 2-3 days after the operation, radiates to the ear and temple, and does not respond well to painkillers.
3 Rules to Lower the Risk of Dry Socket:
1. Do Not Smoke:
§bPhysical Risk:§/b The act of smoking creates a strong negative pressure (vacuum) in the mouth that can "suck" the clot out of place.
§bChemical Risk:§/b The toxins and nicotine in cigarette smoke narrow the blood vessels that make healing possible. They reduce the amount of oxygen and nutrients reaching the wound.
§bSmoking in the first 72 hours (if possible, for 1 week) increases the risk of dry socket.§/b
2. Do Not Spit, Rinse or Use a Straw:
Drinking through a straw, spitting forcefully or rinsing the mouth can dislodge that clot.
Has blood collected in your mouth? Swallow. Do not spit.
Did you drink water? Swallow. Do not swish.
3. Avoid Heat (First 24 Hours):
Hot shower, hot tea, hot soup... Heat widens the blood vessels (vasodilation), increases bleeding and disrupts the healthy structure of the clot. §bFor the first 24 hours, only cold and lukewarm.§/b
Your Post-Surgical Care Plan for the First 72 Hours
1. Gauze Pad and Bleeding Control (First 1-2 Hours)
Keep biting firmly on the sterile gauze pad we told you to bite on when you left our clinic for §bat least 30-45 minutes§/b. It is not enough for it simply to sit there; "pressure" must be applied.

After you remove the gauze, a slight "oozing" or a pinkish tinge in your saliva is normal. If fresh, red blood is coming into your mouth, fold a new sterile gauze pad, place it on the surgical site, and bite on it with pressure for another 45 minutes.
2. Managing Swelling (Edema): Cold Compress (First 48 Hours)
Impacted tooth operations are surgery, and the body reacts to this trauma with "swelling" (edema). This is a normal part of healing.

§bSwelling usually does not peak right after the operation but 24-48 hours later, and begins to go down after the 72nd hour.§/b (So it is normal to wake up on day 2 more swollen than on day 1; do not panic.)
§bRecommendation:§/b To help reduce swelling, start applying a cold compress (ice pack) to the outside of the surgical area (on the cheek) as soon as you get home.
§bCorrect Application:§/b Wrap the ice in a cloth. Hold it for 15 minutes, then rest for 15 minutes. Repeat this cycle as much as you can while you are awake during the first 24-48 hours.
3. Medication Management (Fighting the Pain)
The medications on the prescription Dr. Eren gave you (painkiller, antibiotic, mouthwash if needed) are your healing protocol.

§bTip:§/b Unless your dentist has told you otherwise, take your painkiller as the anesthesia is wearing off, without waiting for the pain to begin. Controlling pain before it starts is generally easier than stopping it after it has started.
If an antibiotic has been prescribed, do not stop it because "I have no pain." To prevent infection, it is essential to finish the whole box that was given (for example, 5-7 days).
4. Oral Hygiene (Keeping the Area Clean)
§bFirst 24 hours: Do not touch the area.§/b Do not brush it, do not use mouthwash, do not even let water hit it. Allow the clot to form.
§bAfter 24 hours:§/b You can brush all your other teeth as usual. A clean mouth supports healing.

If your dentist gave you a mouthwash, start it after 24 hours. Remember: no swishing, no spitting! Take the liquid into your mouth, tilt your head from side to side, and let it run slowly into the sink.
Nutrition Plan for the First 72 Hours
Day 1 (First 24 Hours): Cold and Liquid Period
§bGoal:§/b To protect the clot and stop the bleeding.
§bWhat to Eat:§/b
Cold soups without pieces (cold yogurt soup, blended cold tomato soup)
Yogurt, kefir, ayran (must have no pieces)
Ice cream (plain): the cold effect can be soothing
Milk pudding, pudding, rice pudding (must be cold)
Smoothie (with a spoon): do not use a straw
Days 2 and 3 (48-72 Hours): Lukewarm and Puree Period
The clot is now more stable. The body needs fuel (protein, vitamins) to heal. Continue to avoid heat; lukewarm foods can be eaten.
§bWhat to Eat:§/b
Lukewarm, blended soups (lentil, broccoli, zucchini... must have no pieces)
Mashed potatoes (lukewarm; can be enriched with butter or milk)
Eggs (scrambled or soft-boiled; a good source of protein for healing)
Cheese (soft, mashed white cheese or cream cheese)
Fruit purees (banana, mashed avocado, applesauce)
What to Avoid During the First Week
§bFoods with Small Grains:§/b Rice, bulgur, sesame (simit), quinoa, strawberry and raspberry seeds... These small particles can get into the socket and lead to infection.
§bHard, Crunchy Foods:§/b Bread crust, chips, nuts, biscuits. They cause mechanical trauma to the wound.
§bSticky Foods:§/b Chewing gum, Turkish delight, caramel. They stick to the stitches.
§bAcidic & Spicy Foods:§/b Orange juice, lemon, hot pepper. They can irritate the open wound.
Conclusion: You Focus on Healing
The first 72 hours are the foundation of your healing process. Following these nutrition and care recommendations supports your recovery.

You now know that swelling usually increases over the first 2-3 days and then begins to go down, that slight oozing is normal, but that severe pain (dry socket) is a "warning sign." Listen to your body, and if you have any doubt, call our clinic right away.

3d-rehberli-implant-cerrahisi.title: What Is Guided (3D) Implant Surgery? How Does It Differ from the Freehand Method?
3d-rehberli-implant-cerrahisi.lead: Information about digital planning, the surgical guide and the process.

b.x: Implant treatment is an established method used to replace missing teeth. However, the word §b"surgery"§/b, which is mentioned together with "implant," creates an understandable concern in many patients.
One of the approaches aimed at easing these concerns is §bGuided (3D) Digital Implant Surgery§/b.
What Is Freehand Surgery?
To understand guided surgery, it helps to know the §b"freehand"§/b method, which has long been widely used.

In the freehand method, the position of the implant is determined according to imaging findings and the dentist's clinical assessment. During surgery the gum is opened as far as needed, and the implant site is prepared without using a surgical template.
Points Taken into Consideration:

As in every surgical procedure, in implant surgery too, proximity to anatomical structures such as nerves and sinuses is an important consideration. Two-dimensional imaging shows the position of these structures in a more limited way than three-dimensional assessment. For this reason, when the dentist considers it necessary, three-dimensional imaging and digital planning may be preferred.
What Is Guided (3D) Digital Implant Surgery?

Guided surgery is a protocol that uses data from §bthree-dimensional imaging§/b and §bdigital planning§/b. In this method, the position of the implant is planned on the computer before the operation, and the process proceeds in three stages.
Stage 1: Digital Planning with 3D Tomography (CBCT)

The process begins with §b3D Dental Tomography (CBCT)§/b. The tomography creates a three-dimensional model of the jawbone. On this 3D model, Dr. Emrecan Eren uses computer software to evaluate the course of the nerve canal and the boundaries of the sinus cavities, and digitally plans the angle and depth of the implant.
§bThis planning helps to evaluate in advance the risks that may be encountered during surgery.§/b
Stage 2: Producing the Surgical Guide (3D Printer)

The digital plan is sent to a 3D printer, and a rigid "plate" that fits the patient's mouth is produced from biocompatible resin. On this plate there are sleeves that direct the position, angle and depth where the implant will be placed. This is called a §b"surgical template"§/b.
Stage 3: Surgical Procedure

On the day of surgery, the dentist places this guide in the patient's mouth. In suitable cases, only a small, circular area may be opened at the point shown by the guide (punch technique). §bIn these cases, since no large incision is made, stitches may often not be needed.§/b Which technique is suitable is determined by the condition of the bone and gum.
Possible Advantages for the Patient
1. Planning
3D planning helps to evaluate in advance the position of structures such as the nerve canal and the sinus cavity. The surgical guide aims to support placing the implant in the planned position.
2. Comfort
In suitable cases, work can be done with a smaller surgical area
In these cases, the aim is for there to be less swelling (edema) and bruising
The healing process varies from person to person
3. Duration

Because planning is done before the operation, the surgical procedure time may be shorter in suitable cases. The duration of the procedure varies according to the number of implants and the characteristics of the case.
Conclusion: Planning Matters

Guided surgery is a method that helps carry planning over into the surgical process in implant treatment. As with every method, results depend on factors such as the person's bone structure, general health and oral care.
At our clinic in Lüleburgaz, we evaluate together with you which method is suitable for you, based on the examination and imaging findings.

acil-dis-agrisi-kirik-ilk-yardim.title: What to Do in a Dental Emergency: Severe Toothache or a Broken Tooth (A First Aid Guide Overseen by a Dentist)
acil-dis-agrisi-kirik-ilk-yardim.lead: First aid steps and what to avoid.

b.x: §bEmergency Notice:§/b This is a first aid guide. It does not replace a professional medical examination.
In a life-threatening emergency (difficulty breathing, bleeding that cannot be stopped, high fever), call 112 immediately. For all other dental emergencies, contact your dentist without delay.

A throbbing toothache that starts at midnight and will not let you sleep. A front tooth that breaks or is knocked out after an unfortunate fall. Dental emergencies always come at the most unexpected, most worrying and most painful moments.
In this moment of panic, knowing what to do §bcan make the difference between "permanent damage" and "simple treatment"§/b. Our most important rule: stay calm and call your dentist without delay.
Emergency 1: Severe, Throbbing Toothache (Abscess/Infection)
This is a "pressure" pain that keeps you awake, pounds in your head and responds poorly to painkillers. It is often a sign that an untreated cavity has reached the nerve.
✅ What Should You Do?
§b1. Call Your Dentist:§/b Call our clinic or the nearest emergency dentist right away. This condition does not go away "on its own."
§b2. Rinse with Warm Salt Water:§/b Add a teaspoon of salt to a glass of warm water. Gently rinse your mouth with this solution. Rinsing with salt water may help clean the area and give some relief.

§b3. Cold Compress (from the Outside):§/b Wrap an ice pack in a thin towel. Hold it against the outside of your cheek. Keep it on for 15 minutes, then rest for 15 minutes. Cold may help reduce swelling.

§b4. Painkiller:§/b If you have no known allergy or any condition that prevents you from taking medication, you can use a suitable painkiller after consulting your dentist or pharmacist. Do not exceed the recommended dose.
§b5. Keep Your Head Elevated:§/b Put two pillows under your head to keep it higher than your heart.
❌ What You Should Not Do
§b❌ Do not put aspirin, cologne, alcohol or clove oil on the tooth.§/b These substances can cause gum irritation and chemical burns.
§b❌ Do not apply a hot compress.§/b Heat can make it easier for the infection to spread.
§b❌ Do not take antibiotics without consulting your dentist.§/b Using an unsuitable antibiotic can make the infection more resistant.
Emergency 2: A Broken or Cracked Tooth (Trauma)
✅ What Should You Do?
§b1. Stay Calm and Find the Piece:§/b In some cases, a broken piece of tooth can be bonded back onto the tooth.
§b2. How Should You Store the Piece?§/b • §bPreferred:§/b Cold milk
• §bAlternative:§/b Your own saliva (under the tongue or inside the cheek)
• §bNot suitable:§/b Dry tissue, plain water
§b3. Rinse Your Mouth:§/b Rinse with lukewarm water to clear the blood from the area.
§b4. Stop the Bleeding:§/b Apply gentle pressure with sterile gauze for 10-15 minutes.
§b5. Cold Compress:§/b If there is swelling, apply a cold compress to the outside.
§b6. Call Your Dentist:§/b Call our clinic right away.

§bInformation:§/b If the piece is stored properly and reaches the dentist quickly (within the first few hours), in some cases it may be possible to bond it back onto the tooth with the "bonding" technique.
Emergency 3: A Tooth Knocked Out Completely (Avulsion)
⏰ Time matters: Storing the tooth correctly and getting it to the dentist within the first 30-60 minutes may increase the chance of saving the tooth.
✅ What Needs to Be Done:
§b1. Stay Calm and Find the Tooth§/b

§b2. Where Should You Hold the Tooth?§/b ⚠️ Do not hold the tooth by the root (the yellowish, rough part). Hold the tooth only by the crown (the visible white, shiny enamel part). Touching the root surface can damage the living cells there and reduce the chance of saving the tooth.

§b3. How Should You Clean It?§/b If the tooth is dirty: rinse it gently only under running cold water, without touching the root, for no more than 10 seconds. Do not wash it with soap, do not brush it, do not rub it.
§b4. How Should You Store It?§/b • §bOption 1:§/b If possible, try to put it back in its place (if you are not in a state of panic)
• §bOption 2:§/b Put it in cold milk
• §bOption 3:§/b Keep it under the tongue (if there is no risk of swallowing it)
§b5. See a Dentist Without Delay§/b In this situation time matters; do not wait.
Conclusion: An Emergency Is a Result
A throbbing abscess is, in many cases, the result of an untreated cavity. A broken tooth, on the other hand, can sometimes be associated with an underlying tooth-clenching problem.

The right first aid helps you manage the moment. The examination and diagnosis that follow aim to identify and treat the root problem that caused the emergency and to reduce the risk of similar situations happening again.
If you have a dental emergency in Lüleburgaz, do not panic. Stay calm, follow the steps in this guide and call our clinic right away.

agiz-kokusu-nedenleri-cozumleri.title: What Causes Bad Breath (Halitosis) and How Is It Addressed?
agiz-kokusu-nedenleri-cozumleri.lead: Causes of VSCs, sources inside the mouth and treatment approaches.

b.x: Bad breath (known in medical terms as "halitosis") is a health problem that is very common in society but is usually "covered up" because of its social and psychological effects. It can make you hesitate to talk with people at close range and keep looking for gum or mints, and so §bit can directly affect your self-confidence§/b.
§bGood to know:§/b In most cases, chronic bad breath does not come from the stomach but directly from hidden sources "inside the mouth."
The Scientific Source of the Bad Smell: "VSCs"

The cause of chronic odor is a special group of bacteria called "anaerobic bacteria" (bacteria that like an oxygen-free environment). These bacteria consume food debris and proteins and release gases as a "waste product" of their digestion.
These gases are called §b"Volatile Sulfur Compounds" (VSC)§/b. These gases (hydrogen sulfide, methyl mercaptan) smell like "rotten eggs" or "spoiled cabbage."
§bSolution:§/b The point is not to "mask" this smell with a perfumed mouthwash, but to find where these bacteria are hiding and treat that source.
Causes Inside the Mouth
1. The Back of the Tongue (A Common Source)
§bWhy:§/b The back surface of your tongue is made up of thousands of indentations and projections called "papillae." These deep grooves act like a "carpet" for food debris, dead cells and bacteria.
§bSolution:§/b Using a "tongue scraper" every morning helps mechanically clean this coating.
2. Periodontitis (Gum Disease)

§bBacterial Nest:§/b This disease creates deep spaces between the tooth and the gum called "periodontal pockets." The bottom of these pockets has no oxygen and is exactly the ideal "nest" for the bacteria that produce VSCs.
§bOdor:§/b The odor of periodontitis is a typical, heavy VSC smell, metallic and mixed with a "smell of blood."
§bSolution:§/b This odor usually does not go away with mouthwash. Depending on the dentist's evaluation, the bottom of the pockets may need to be cleaned with "curettage (deep cleaning)."
3. Untreated Cavities and Old Leaking Fillings
§bProblem:§/b The inside of decayed cavities is full of food debris and bacteria. They cannot be brushed. While this food "rots" there, it produces VSCs.
The same risk applies to old fillings that have "marginal leakage."
4. Impacted Wisdom Teeth (Pericoronitis)
§bProblem:§/b Under the "hood" over a partially erupted wisdom tooth, a "pocket" forms where food gets trapped and where the brush has difficulty reaching.
§bSolution:§/b Depending on the dentist's evaluation, that wisdom tooth may need to be surgically removed.
5. Ill-Fitting/Old Dentures and Bridges

§bProblem:§/b If the edge of an "old" or "ill-fitting" bridge does not fit the gum properly, plaque builds up in that gap. Removable dentures are porous structures and turn into a nest for bacteria if they are not cared for properly.
Causes Outside the Mouth (Systemic)
If none of the causes above is present in your mouth, we look for the source of the odor "outside the mouth":
Ear, Nose and Throat (ENT) Related:
§bSinusitis:§/b Chronic sinus infections and postnasal drip
§bTonsil Stones:§/b Extremely foul-smelling stones that collect in the crypts of the tonsils
Systemic Diseases (A Serious Signal):
§bDiabetes:§/b Uncontrolled diabetes, an "acetone" smell on the breath
§bKidney Failure:§/b An "ammonia" smell on the breath
§bLiver Failure:§/b A "musty" or "sweetish-sulfurous" smell
§bStomach (Reflux - GERD):§/b Stomach acid flowing back, a sour smell
Lifestyle:
§bGarlic, Onion:§/b Temporary; after being digested they enter the bloodstream
§bSmoking and Alcohol:§/b They contribute to dry mouth and increase the risk of periodontitis
Why Do Gum and Mouthwash Not Work?
The problem is trying to mask the "bacterial gas" with the "mint" flavor in a mouthwash. This does not treat the source of the odor.
§bWarning:§/b Alcohol-based mouthwashes dry the mucous membrane inside the mouth. Saliva may decrease, bacterial growth may increase, and the odor may get even worse.
How Do We Evaluate It in the Clinic?
Step 1: Diagnosis
We listen: When did the odor start? Is there any stomach complaint?
We examine: Is the back of your tongue coated?
We measure: We measure the gums with a periodontal probe. Are there pockets?
We image: When necessary, with radiographic imaging, is there hidden decay, a leaking filling or an impacted tooth?
Step 2: Treating the Root Cause
§bTongue Coating:§/b Tongue scraper training and professional cleaning
§bGingivitis:§/b Professional tartar (calculus) cleaning
§bPeriodontitis:§/b Curettage (deep cleaning)
§bDecay/Leakage:§/b Filling/crown under the microscope
§bWisdom Tooth:§/b Surgical removal
Step 3: Holistic Referral
If no cause that explains the odor is found in your oral examination, we refer you to an ENT specialist or an Internal Medicine/Gastroenterology specialist to find the underlying systemic cause.
Conclusion: Fresh Breath Is a Sign of Health Earned

Chronic bad breath is not a source of "shame" but a "medical signal" your body is giving you. "Silencing" this signal with gum, mints or alcohol-based mouthwashes means allowing a serious infection, such as underlying gum disease or decay, to progress.
At our clinic in Lüleburgaz, finding these hidden bacterial nests and planning treatment aimed at the source is part of our "Holistic Health" approach.

amalgam-kompozit-dolgu-karsilastirma.title: Amalgam (Silver) Fillings or Composite (Tooth-Colored) Fillings? A Comparison
amalgam-kompozit-dolgu-karsilastirma.lead: A comparison in terms of safety, durability, aesthetics and the minimally invasive approach.

b.x: When it comes to treating tooth decay, there is a classic dilemma that our patients have heard about for decades: "black" or "silver" amalgam fillings, known for their durability, or "white" composite fillings, which stand out for their aesthetics?

We also know that in recent years there has been growing concern about the §b"mercury"§/b in amalgam fillings. The question "Should I have these fillings removed?" has become one of the questions we hear most often in our clinic.
What Is an Amalgam Filling?

An amalgam filling is a durable metal alloy that has been used in dentistry for many years. It is made by mixing metals such as silver, tin, copper and zinc with mercury. Mercury plays the role of a "carrier" and "binder" that holds these metal powders together.
Advantages of Amalgam Fillings:
§bDurability:§/b It is resistant to wear and, under suitable conditions, can stay in the mouth for many years.
§bEase of Placement:§/b It is relatively simple to place.
§bTechnical Tolerance:§/b Unlike composite fillings, it is not greatly affected by slight moisture such as saliva.
Disadvantages of Amalgam Fillings:
1. Aesthetic Problem:
Its metallic gray/black color creates an aesthetic concern, especially in the smile line, and over time it can stain the tooth gray from the inside.
2. Mercury Concern:
Yes, amalgam fillings contain mercury. However, mercury is not in a "free" state within this alloy; it is bound to the other metals.
The amount of mercury vapor released from intact amalgam fillings during chewing is at a low level. You can discuss your personal concerns on this subject with your dentist.
3. The Real Technical Problem: "Not Minimally Invasive"

This is the most important technical disadvantage that does not fit our "Minimally Invasive Approach" philosophy. §bAn amalgam filling does not bond chemically to the tooth§/b. For it to stay in the tooth, the dentist needs to create mechanical retention areas called "undercuts." This means: §bTo place an amalgam, part of the healthy tooth structure that is not decayed may also need to be removed.§/b
What Is a Composite Filling? ("White" Filling)

Composite fillings (or "light-cured fillings") are tooth-colored aesthetic materials. They consist of "resin," which forms the natural structure of the tooth, and "ceramic/glass" particles embedded in it.
Unlike amalgam, a composite filling is not mechanically "wedged" into the tooth; it bonds to the tooth micro-mechanically and chemically by using special "bonding" agents.
Advantages of Composite Fillings:
1. Minimally Invasive Approach (Our Philosophy):

This is an important advantage of composite fillings. Because it can bond to the tooth, the dentist generally does not need to create an "undercut." In this way, §bessentially the decayed tissue is cleaned and the healthy tooth structure is preserved as much as possible.§/b
2. Aesthetics:
It can be matched to the natural color of the tooth. With the layering technique, the natural balance of "translucency" and "opacity" of the tooth can be imitated.
3. Biocompatibility (A Mercury-Free Solution):
It contains no metal or mercury. It may be an option for people with metal sensitivity.
4. Strengthening the Tooth:
Because it bonds chemically to the tooth, it supports the remaining structure of the tooth and can increase its "fracture resistance."
The "Weak Point" of Composite Fillings and Our Clinic's Solution
There is a perception that composite fillings are less durable. This perception is partly true, but the reason is not the material itself but §b"the application technique."§/b
Disadvantage: Technical Sensitivity

Composite fillings require a dry and controlled working environment. The main risk factor is §bmoisture§/b (saliva, blood, breath vapor). If moisture contaminates the tooth surface during the bonding procedure, adhesion can be adversely affected.
Our Approach: Why Composite Fillings Under Magnification?
In our clinic, to manage this technical sensitivity, we place importance on working under magnification.
§bIsolation:§/b Under magnification, we aim to isolate the tooth from moisture with a rubber dam.
§bControlled Decay Removal:§/b The microscope helps the boundary between decayed and healthy tissue be seen more clearly.
§bCareful Bonding:§/b We apply bonding agents with care.
§bMargin Adaptation:§/b To reduce the risk of leakage, the margins of the filling are checked under magnification.
§bNote:§/b How long a filling will function depends on many factors, such as oral hygiene, eating habits, tooth clenching and regular check-ups.
"Should I Have My Old Amalgam Fillings Removed?" (An Honest Answer)
§bOur answer:§/b Removing intact amalgam fillings that are not fractured and do not have marginal leakage solely because of mercury concerns is generally not recommended.
§bWhy?§/b Because the release of mercury vapor can temporarily increase while an amalgam filling is being removed.
In Which Situations Do We Remove Them in Our Clinic?
§bMedical Necessity:§/b If we have found new decay under the filling
§bFracture or Leakage:§/b If the filling itself or its margin has broken
§bAesthetic Request:§/b If the patient makes an informed request for a change
When the decision to remove an amalgam is made, we carry out the procedure with protective measures (isolation with a rubber dam, high-volume suction, removal in large pieces).
Conclusion: A Protective and Aesthetic Approach

Amalgam fillings are a durable material that has been widely used in dentistry for many years. Composite fillings, on the other hand, offer an option §baimed at aesthetics and preserving tooth structure§/b.

As the Dr. Emrecan Eren Polyclinic, our philosophy is based on "Minimally Invasive," "Aesthetic" and "Biocompatible" approaches. For this reason, where suitable, we give priority to evaluating composite fillings, which aim to preserve healthy tooth structure and which we place carefully under magnification.

bruksizm-dis-sikma-belirtileri.title: Do You Wake Up with Jaw Pain in the Morning? These Symptoms May Be a Sign of Bruxism

b.x: The alarm rings, you wake up, but you do not feel "rested." In your cheeks, your temples or just in front of your ears there is a §b"dull" and "tired" ache§/b. Even opening your jaw or yawning is uncomfortable. You start the day with a headache.

If this scenario sounds familiar, you are not alone. Quite possibly, while you should have been in deep sleep all night, your jaw muscles were "working overtime." In medical terms we call this condition §b"Bruxism" (Teeth Clenching or Grinding)§/b.
What Is Bruxism? (Clenching vs. Grinding)
Bruxism is the involuntary contact, clenching or grinding of the teeth outside of their normal functions. It has two main types:
Clenching
The "silent" and more "common" type
"Locking" the teeth together and applying high vertical pressure
The force applied can be well above normal chewing force
The main culprit behind morning jaw pain
Grinding
The "noisy" type
Rubbing the teeth together by sliding the jaw side to side or back and forth
Usually noticed by a partner
It physically "files down," wears away and cracks tooth enamel
The type that requires particular attention is §bSleep Bruxism§/b, because it can occur outside our conscious control, for long periods and with high forces.
Why Do We Clench Our Teeth? (3 Main Causes)
1. Stress, Anxiety and Lifestyle (The Most Common)
Daily stress and anxiety are among the factors often associated with bruxism. This tension can show itself as involuntary contraction of the jaw muscles during sleep.
§bIn other words, the stress you experience during the day can be reflected in your jaw at night.§/b
2. Sleep Disorders (May Cause No Symptoms)
§bSleep Apnea:§/b Sleep apnea, in which breathing repeatedly stops during sleep, may be associated with teeth grinding in some people.
If you snore and wake up feeling "tired" in the mornings, the cause of your bruxism may be sleep apnea.
3. Occlusal (Bite) Factors
A filling or crown that has been made "higher" than it should be
"Early contact" between teeth
Severe crowding
Symptom Checklist
Muscle and Joint Pain:
Pain and fatigue in the cheek muscles on waking in the morning
Tenderness in the jaw joint just in front of the ear
"Tension-type headache" spreading to the temples
Stiffness in the neck and shoulder muscles
Physical Damage to the Teeth:
§bWear:§/b Teeth becoming shorter and flattened
§bAbfraction:§/b Notch-shaped defects where the tooth meets the gum
§bCracks and Fractures:§/b Unexplained cracks in filled or otherwise intact teeth
Other Signs:
Biting the inside of the cheek (a white, rough line)
Scalloped edges on the tongue
Ringing in the ears (tinnitus)
A "clicking" sound from the jaw
What Happens If It Is Not Treated?
§bTooth Damage:§/b Worn teeth may become sensitive, crack or break
§bAesthetic Changes:§/b The front teeth becoming shorter
§bTemporomandibular Joint (TMJ) Problems:§/b Pain, noises in the joint or limited mouth opening
§bHeadache:§/b Recurrent headaches and reduced sleep quality
The Solution: Protection and Addressing the Cause
1. Protection (Occlusal Splint - Night Guard)
It is one of the frequently used protective treatment options. In our clinic it is a stabilization splint made of hard acrylic and planned with digital design.
§bIts role:§/b It acts as a "shield" that protects the teeth from wear and relaxes the jaw muscles.
2. The Root Cause (Holistic Approach)
§bLifestyle:§/b Stress management, reducing caffeine, sleep hygiene
§bBite Analysis:§/b Occlusion analysis with digital design
§bSpecialist Referral:§/b An ENT or sleep specialist if sleep apnea is suspected
Conclusion: Take Morning Jaw Pain Seriously
Waking up with jaw pain in the morning is not a "normal part of a stressful life." It is a clear "warning signal" from your body.
When this signal is ignored, your teeth, your jaw joint and your quality of life can be adversely affected in the long term.
