cerrahi-dis-cekimi-farklari.title: What Are the Differences Between a Surgical Tooth Extraction and a Normal (Simple) Tooth Extraction?
cerrahi-dis-cekimi-farklari.lead: Reasons for surgical extraction, the process and the healing period.

b.x: After your examination with your dentist, you learned that you have a tooth that needs to be removed, and your dentist said this procedure needs to be a §b"surgical extraction"§/b rather than a "normal extraction."

The word "surgical" alone can create the perception of something "more complicated" and "more painful." §bThe short answer:§/b A "surgical extraction" does not always mean "more painful." It means a "more precise," "more planned" and "more controlled" approach to removing a difficult tooth.
What Is a Normal (Simple) Tooth Extraction?
A normal, simple or "uncomplicated" tooth extraction is the most commonly performed procedure. For this procedure to be done, the tooth must meet "ideal" conditions:
§bVisibility:§/b The tooth is above the gum level (fully erupted)
§bAccessibility:§/b There is enough sound crown for the dentist to grasp with forceps
§bAnatomy:§/b The roots of the tooth are straight, not excessively curved or fused to the bone
How Does the Procedure Work?
§bAnesthesia:§/b The area is numbed with local anesthesia
§bLoosening:§/b The tooth is gently moved within its socket with an elevator
§bRemoval:§/b The tooth is grasped with forceps and removed in one piece
§bClosing:§/b A sterile gauze pad is placed; stitches are usually not needed
What Is a Surgical Tooth Extraction?
§bDo not let the word "surgical" frighten you.§/b It means a "more precise," "more planned" and "more controlled" approach.
§bThe Basic Difference:§/b A surgical extraction is generally a procedure that requires opening a small, controlled "window" in the gum (raising a flap) to reach the tooth.

All of these procedures, as with a normal extraction, are done under local anesthesia; the aim is for no pain to be felt during the procedure. The only difference is that the dentist needs more visibility, more space and more precision.
Which Teeth Require Surgical Extraction?
1. Impacted or Partially Impacted Teeth
§bThe Most Common Reason:§/b Teeth that have not found room in the jaw and remain under the gum or bone, above all impacted wisdom teeth.
§bProblem:§/b There is no "crown" to hold with forceps. To reach the tooth, it is usually necessary to open this "window."
2. Broken Roots or Severely Decayed Teeth
§bProblem:§/b The decay has progressed so far that the visible part of the tooth has broken off completely. Only the roots remain.
§bSolution:§/b The gum needs to be opened in order to remove the roots safely.
3. Complex Root Anatomy
§bProblem:§/b The roots of the tooth may be "hook-like," curved in an "S" shape or "widely spread apart."

§bDigital Planning:§/b In difficult extractions that the dentist considers necessary, 3D dental tomography (CBCT) may be requested. This image helps in the three-dimensional evaluation of the root anatomy and its relationship with surrounding structures.
4. Teeth Fused to the Bone (Ankylosis)
§bProblem:§/b The root of the tooth "fuses directly to the jawbone" (ankylosis).
§bResult:§/b It is usually not possible to remove this tooth by "rocking" it out. The tooth must be separated from the bone surgically.
5. Presence of a Cyst or Abscess
§bProblem:§/b There may be a large cyst or chronic abscess at the root of the tooth that needs to be cleaned out.
§bSolution:§/b A surgical approach is needed so that the cyst tissue can be cleaned out.
The Surgical Extraction Process Step by Step
Step 1: Planning and Anesthesia

When necessary, the procedure is planned with 3D tomography. The area is numbed with local anesthesia. §bThe aim is that no pain is felt during the procedure thanks to local anesthesia; a sensation of pressure may be felt.§/b
Step 2: Access (Gingival Flap)
A "window" is opened in the gum, kept as small as possible, that allows access to the root of the tooth.
Step 3: Freeing the Tooth
§bSectioning the Tooth:§/b This procedure, which makes patients worry "they broke my tooth," is in fact a planned surgical technique.
Removing the tooth in one piece may in some cases require more force and the removal of more bone
Dividing the tooth in two or three and removing it in small pieces aims to reduce the force applied and the intervention on the surrounding bone
The purpose of sectioning the tooth is to reduce trauma to the tissues.
Step 4: Closing and Stitches
The wound area is cleaned meticulously. The "window" we opened is gently returned to its original place and secured with 1-2 small stitches.
The Healing Process: Is It Different After a Surgical Extraction?
Yes, the healing process after a surgical extraction is somewhat different, because there is more tissue for your body to repair:
After a Simple Extraction
• Usually mild pain
• Usually mild swelling
• Usually no stitches
After a Surgical Extraction
• Swelling and bruising (common and expected)
• Pain (can be managed with painkillers)
• Stitch care is needed
• The first 72 hours are critical
Care Rules (Important):
Cold compress (for swelling)
Regular use of the medications recommended by your dentist
To reduce the risk of dry socket: do not smoke, do not spit
Conclusion: "Surgical" = "Planned Intervention"
The term "surgical extraction" may sound frightening; however, it is a planned method chosen according to the characteristics of the tooth.

It means removing, in a planned way and under local anesthesia, with care to protect the tissues, a tooth that the examination and necessary imaging have shown to be difficult to remove by normal means.
At our clinic in Lüleburgaz, we make the decision for a surgical extraction based on the examination and imaging findings, and we explain the process to you in detail.
§bAbout the Author:§/b This article was written and medically reviewed by §bDr. Emrecan Eren§/b. Our clinic provides care to its patients with evidence-based treatment protocols.

dis-beyazlatma-sonrasi-bakim.title: The First 48 Hours After Teeth Whitening: White Diet and Care Recommendations
dis-beyazlatma-sonrasi-bakim.lead: Dietary and care recommendations that help keep your whitening result for longer.

b.x: You have completed professional teeth whitening (bleaching). There is one period that is especially important for keeping the result: §bthe first 48 hours§/b.
This period can affect how well the new shade is maintained. For this reason, it is important to follow the aftercare recommendations.

This guide explains why a "White Diet" is recommended during the first 48 hours after whitening, how you can manage sensitivity, and which foods you should avoid. This short period of attention helps the result last longer.
Why Are the First 48 Hours Important?
Once you understand how teeth whitening works, you will better understand why a "White Diet" is recommended.

Professional whitening agents (hydrogen peroxide or carbamide peroxide) §bpenetrate the enamel§/b, the outermost layer of your tooth. These agents chemically break down the colored pigments (chromogens) that have built up over the years in the microscopic pores of the enamel (dentin tubules). This process temporarily makes the enamel more §b"porous"§/b and permeable.

At the same time, the whitening process temporarily removes the natural protective protein layer of your teeth, called the §b"pellicle"§/b. It takes about §b48 hours§/b for this layer to re-form and for the enamel to stabilize.
During this period, teeth may take up strong staining agents (coffee, tea, wine) more easily than usual. The purpose of the "White Diet" is to reduce the risk of re-staining during this time.
The "White Diet" Rule: List of Things to Avoid
For the first 48-72 hours, your basic rule should be simple: §b"Anything that could stain a white T-shirt can also stain your teeth."§/b
It is recommended that you avoid the following foods and drinks during this time:
1. Dark-Colored and Acidic Drinks
§bCoffee:§/b Contains a lot of tannin and dark pigment. The answer to "Can I add milk?" is unfortunately no; the risk remains.
§bTea:§/b Black tea in particular is a strong staining agent. Green tea and herbal teas can also cause staining during this period.
§bRed Wine:§/b It combines acidity and dark pigment.
§bCola and All Carbonated Drinks:§/b They both stain and contain high levels of acid (phosphoric acid), making the enamel even more sensitive.
§bColored Fruit Juices:§/b All acidic and pigmented juices, such as sour cherry, pomegranate, and orange juice.
2. Colored Sauces and Foods
§bTomato Sauce and Tomato Paste:§/b Red pigment and high acidity.
§bSoy Sauce, Ketchup, Mustard:§/b All colored sauces.
§bBeets, Red Cabbage, Carrots:§/b Vegetables that contain intense natural pigments.
§bDark-Colored Fruits:§/b Strawberries, blackberries, sour cherries, cherries, black mulberries.
§bChocolate and Cocoa:§/b In all forms.
§bTurmeric and Curry:§/b These are strong staining spices.
3. Cigarettes and All Tobacco Products

It is recommended that you avoid smoking during the 48 hours after whitening. The tar and nicotine in tobacco can cause §byellow-brown staining§/b on teeth during this period and may negatively affect the whitening result.
What You Can Eat: "White Diet" Menu Suggestions
So, "What will we eat?" Although this list may look restrictive, it covers only a short period.
Permitted Protein Sources
Boiled or grilled chicken breast (without sauce)
Smoked turkey (without sauce)
White fish (whiting, sea bass - not fried)
Egg white (the yolk contains pigment and should be avoided for the first 48 hours)
Tofu (without sauce)
Permitted Dairy Products and Grains
Milk
Plain (white) yogurt, plain kefir
White cheese, curd cheese (lor), kashar cheese (except aged kashar)
Rice (preferably soft and porridge-like) and rice flour
Pasta (without sauce or cream; perhaps with a very little salt and olive oil)
Oatmeal (cooked with milk, without fruit)
The soft inside of white bread (not the crust)
Permitted Vegetables and Fruits
Cauliflower (boiled)
White potato (boiled or mashed)
Banana
Apple (peeled and eaten carefully)
Permitted Drinks
§bWater:§/b Can be consumed freely throughout the day.
§bMineral Water:§/b Plain, non-acidic or low-acid types may be preferred.
§bMilk:§/b Can be consumed as a snack.
Sensitivity After Teeth Whitening: Is It Normal and How Is It Managed?
Another topic patients often ask about is §bsensitivity§/b. Sudden, brief twinges or sensitivity to cold in the teeth during the first 24-48 hours after whitening are common and usually expected.

As mentioned earlier, the cause of this sensitivity is that the enamel temporarily becomes porous and the dentin tubules are exposed. This makes the nerve endings more sensitive to external stimuli (especially cold air or drinks).
The following steps may be recommended to help you get through this period more comfortably:
Tips for Managing Sensitivity:
§bDesensitizing Toothpastes:§/b Start using toothpastes specially made for sensitivity, containing potassium nitrate or stannous fluoride, from 1 week before the treatment and after it.
§bUse of Pain Relievers:§/b If sensitivity affects your daily comfort, you can use a pain reliever recommended by your dentist (usually one containing ibuprofen).
§bLukewarm Liquids:§/b Avoid very hot or very cold foods and drinks for the first 48 hours. Room-temperature or lukewarm liquids will make you more comfortable.
§bFluoride Application:§/b When needed, a professional fluoride varnish that helps reduce sensitivity can be applied at our clinic.
This sensitivity is usually §btemporary§/b and in most cases decreases within a few days. If the sensitivity lasts a long time or is severe, contact your dentist.
Conclusion: The Role of Aftercare
The first 48 hours of the "White Diet" and aftercare complement professional teeth whitening. This short period of attention may help the color you have achieved last longer.
Paying attention to these small details contributes to keeping the result for longer.
§bAbout the Author:§/b This article was written and medically reviewed by §bDr. Emrecan Eren§/b. Our clinic provides care to its patients with evidence-based treatment protocols.

dis-eti-cekilmesi.title: What Causes Gum Recession? Symptoms and Treatment Options
dis-eti-cekilmesi.lead: If your teeth look longer than they used to: the causes, the risks, and what can be done.

b.x: Gum recession is the edge of the gum pulling back toward the tooth root and exposing the root surface. Because it usually progresses slowly, it may take a while to notice. Teeth §blooking longer§/b than before, sensitivity at the neck of the tooth, or gaps between the teeth becoming more noticeable can be the first signs.
Causes of Gum Recession
§bGum disease (periodontitis):§/b Inflammation caused by tartar and bacterial plaque can lead to loss of the bone and gum that support the tooth.
§bHard brushing:§/b A stiff-bristled brush and horizontal, forceful brushing can wear down the gum.
§bThin gum structure:§/b In some people the gum is naturally thin and more prone to recession.
§bClenching and grinding:§/b Excessive force on the teeth can contribute to wear at the neck of the tooth.
§bSmoking:§/b Increases the risk of gum disease and negatively affects healing.
§bPosition of the teeth:§/b The gum can be thinner around crowded teeth or teeth positioned toward the outside of the bone.
Which Symptoms Should You Watch For?
Twinges at the neck of the tooth with cold and heat
Teeth appearing longer
Gum bleeding when brushing
A feeling of looseness in the teeth
Bad breath
To Slow Its Progress
Use a soft-bristled brush and brush without pressing hard.
Clean between your teeth every day with dental floss or interdental brushes.
Have your tartar removed at regular check-ups.
Quitting smoking has a positive effect on gum health.
Treatment Options
Treatment is planned according to the cause of the recession and how far it has progressed. At the examination, gum pockets are measured and, if needed, bone support is evaluated with an X-ray.
§bTartar removal and deep cleaning (curettage):§/b For recession caused by gum disease, controlling the inflammation is the first step.
§bCorrecting brushing habits:§/b For recession caused by mechanical wear, this slows its progress.
§bCovering wear at the neck of the tooth with a filling:§/b May reduce sensitivity.
§bGum grafts:§/b In suitable cases, surgical procedures can be planned to cover the exposed root surface.
§bNight guard:§/b May be recommended if clenching is also present.
Conclusion

When gum recession is noticed early, its progress can often be slowed by removing the cause. If you notice that your teeth look longer or that the necks of your teeth are sensitive, a gum examination is recommended.
This content is for general information only; please consult your dentist for diagnosis and treatment.

dis-eti-kanamasi-nedenleri.title: What Causes Bleeding Gums? Is It the First Sign of a Serious Problem?
dis-eti-kanamasi-nedenleri.lead: The difference between gingivitis and periodontitis, and treatment options.

b.x: Seeing a pink or red stain in the sink while brushing your teeth in the morning can be worrying. Most people's first reaction is: "I must have brushed too hard."
§bHealthy gums do not usually bleed with normal brushing.§/b Bleeding gums are more often an important "warning signal" of inflammation already present in that area than of hard brushing.
The Cause of Bleeding: Your Body's Warning Signal

To understand bleeding gums, it helps to know how your body works. What happens when a splinter gets stuck in your finger? Your body urgently sends blood to the area to get rid of that "foreign" invader.
For your gums, the "splinter" is the sticky layer of bacteria called §b"bacterial plaque"§/b.
How the Process Works:
§bPlaque Buildup:§/b When food debris stays on the tooth surface, bacteria multiply and form a sticky film called "plaque".
§bRelease of Toxins:§/b The bacteria in this plaque release "toxins" that irritate your gums.
§bThe Body's Response:§/b Your body sends "fighter" blood cells to the area to fight this bacterial invasion.
§bResult: Bleeding.§/b Gums that fill with blood, swell, and turn red can bleed easily even with the light touch of a toothbrush.
So bleeding gums are not a "disease" in themselves but §b"a sign of disease."§/b Bleeding is the body's reaction to inflammation in the gum and shows that an examination is needed.
Is It a Serious Problem? (Stage 1: Gingivitis - A Reversible Warning)
§bGingivitis (Gum Inflammation)§/b is the first, "reversible" stage of this problem.
What Is It?
The infection and inflammation are only in the gum. It has not yet spread to the jawbone that supports the tooth.
Symptoms:
The gums are red, shiny, and swollen
They bleed easily when brushing or flossing
There is usually no pain
The Good News:
Gingivitis §bcan usually be reversed with treatment in its early stage§/b. At this stage, permanent bone loss has not yet begun.
§bTreatment:§/b A professional tartar cleaning removes all bacterial plaque and tartar in the area. Combined with good home care, the gums show improvement in a short time in most cases.
The "Serious Problem" Begins (Stage 2: Periodontitis - The Destruction Stage)
What happens if you ignore the "warning signal" of the gingivitis stage? The infection goes deeper.
§bPeriodontitis (Gum Disease)§/b is the second, "serious" and "irreversible" stage of this problem.
What Is It?
The infection is no longer only in the gum. It has spread to the "periodontal ligaments" that support the tooth and, most importantly, to the §b"jawbone"§/b.
Symptoms:
Heavy and sometimes spontaneous gum bleeding
Bad breath and a metallic taste in the mouth
Gum recession (teeth looking "long")
Pus coming from between the teeth and gums
Loose or shifting teeth
The Bad News:
§bBone loss caused by periodontitis usually does not come back on its own§/b.
§bTreatment:§/b At this stage a simple tartar cleaning is often not enough. Advanced gum treatment (curettage) or surgical procedures may be needed.
Other Causes: Systemic Factors
The most common cause of bleeding gums is plaque and tartar. However, other factors can also play a role:
Hormonal Changes:
Especially during pregnancy or adolescence, hormone fluctuations can exaggerate the gums' reaction to plaque.
Systemic Diseases:
§bDiabetes:§/b Diabetes can make it harder for the body to fight infection and can increase the risk of gum disease.
§bBlood Disorders:§/b Leukemia or blood clotting disorders can cause gums to bleed for no apparent reason.
Medication Use:
Some blood pressure medications or epilepsy medications can cause gum overgrowth and, therefore, bleeding.
What Should You Do? (A 4-Step Action Plan)
1. Do Not Stop Brushing
The thought "It bleeds, so I won't touch it" is a common mistake. You should brush the bleeding area more softly and gently, but more effectively.
2. Use the Right Equipment:
Be sure to use a §bsoft§/b or extra-soft-bristled toothbrush.
3. Start Flossing:
Most bleeding starts at the "contact surfaces between teeth" that the brush cannot reach. If you bleed when you floss, this may show that the area needs cleaning.
4. Dental Examination (The Important Step):
What you do at home is only "first aid". Only a dentist can tell whether the problem is gingivitis or periodontitis.
Conclusion: Bleeding Is Your Body's "Check Engine" Light
When the "oil light" comes on in your car's dashboard, you don't cover it with tape and keep driving. Bleeding gums are your mouth's §b"check engine" light§/b.
Ignoring it by saying "I brushed too hard" can open the way to a broader process that may end in periodontitis, bone loss, loose teeth, and even tooth loss.
For this reason, it is important to notice the problem early, while it is still at the gingivitis stage, and to have it treated.
§bAbout the Author:§/b This article was written and medically reviewed by §bDr. Emrecan Eren§/b. Our clinic provides care to its patients with evidence-based treatment protocols.

dis-hassasiyeti-nedenleri.title: What Causes Tooth Sensitivity? Teeth That Twinge With Cold and Heat
dis-hassasiyeti-nedenleri.lead: The most common causes of sensitivity, what can be done at home, and signs that need an examination.

b.x: If you feel a brief, sharp twinge in a tooth with a cold drink, hot tea, or something sweet, this is most often §bdentin sensitivity§/b. When the enamel that protects the outer surface of the tooth or the gum that covers the root recedes, the dentin layer underneath is exposed. Very fine channels in the dentin carry the stimulus to the nerve of the tooth, and you feel the twinge.
Common Causes of Tooth Sensitivity
§bGum recession:§/b The root surface is exposed; there is no protective enamel on the root surface.
§bHard brush and hard brushing:§/b Over time, the enamel and gum can wear down.
§bClenching and grinding (bruxism):§/b Can cause wear on the enamel and notches at the neck of the tooth.
§bAcidic foods and drinks:§/b Frequently consumed acidic drinks can soften the enamel.
§bCavity or broken filling:§/b If sensitivity is in a single tooth and gradually increasing, a cavity should be considered.
§bRecent treatments:§/b Sensitivity lasting a few days can occur after a filling, tartar cleaning, or whitening.
What Can Be Done at Home?
Use a soft-bristled toothbrush and brush with circular motions without pressing hard.
Use toothpastes made for sensitivity regularly; their effect usually becomes noticeable within a few weeks.
After acidic drinks, rinse your mouth with water and wait a while instead of brushing right away.
If you think you clench your teeth at night, mention it at your examination.
When Should You See a Dentist?
The following situations may be more than just sensitivity and need an examination:
Pain that lasts a long time after the stimulus is gone
Pain that starts on its own or wakes you at night
Sensitivity in a single tooth that is gradually increasing
Swelling in the gum or pain when chewing
These symptoms can be a sign of a cavity or inflammation of the tooth nerve and may require a filling or root canal treatment.
Which Treatments Are Applied at the Clinic?
Protective varnish or fluoride applied to sensitive surfaces
Covering an exposed root surface or wear at the neck of the tooth with a composite filling
A filling if there is a cavity, and root canal treatment if the nerve is affected
A night guard if there is clenching
Treatments for gum recession in suitable cases
Conclusion

A brief twinge that starts and ends with a stimulus often eases with simple measures. If the sensitivity is concentrated in a single tooth, lasts a long time, or starts on its own, its cause needs to be determined by an examination.
This content is for general information only; please consult your dentist for diagnosis and treatment.

dis-tasi-temizligi-zarar-verir-mi.title: Does Tartar Removal (Scaling) Damage Teeth? Common Misconceptions
dis-tasi-temizligi-zarar-verir-mi.lead: Misconceptions about enamel scratching, sensitivity, and loose teeth.

b.x: In dentistry, professional tartar removal is perhaps the treatment around which the most "urban legends" have been created. We hear these concerns from many patients who come to our clinic: §b"Cleaning scratches the enamel," "The spaces between my teeth opened up," "My teeth started to wobble more."§/b

§bShort answer:§/b Professional tartar removal performed with the correct technique is not expected to harm the teeth. On the contrary, it is an important medical procedure that aims to rid your teeth and gums of the actual harmful agent, tartar.
First, Let's Get to Know the Enemy: What Is Tartar (Calculus)?
To understand why tartar removal is not harmful, we need to know exactly what "tartar" is.
How It Forms:
§bPlaque Formation:§/b After every meal, a soft, sticky film of bacteria called "bacterial plaque" forms on the surface of your teeth.

§bHardening (Calcification):§/b If this soft plaque is not cleaned regularly, calcium and phosphate minerals in your saliva settle into the plaque and over time turn it into a hard structure called "tartar".
§bThe Toothbrush Falls Short:§/b This structure is now "mineralized bacterial plaque" and sticks firmly to the tooth surface. It usually cannot be removed with a toothbrush.
Tartar is not only a cosmetic problem. Its surface is porous and creates an ideal "anchoring" area for more plaque. The bacteria living on it can cause §binflammation of the gums§/b.
Does the Procedure Scratch the Enamel? (How Does Ultrasonic Cleaning Work?)
One concern patients often raise is "that tool that scratches the enamel". This is a common misconception about the procedure.
How Does the Ultrasonic Scaler Work?
Ultrasonic scalers are used in tartar removal. Patients may confuse the tip of this instrument with the "drill" used for fillings. In fact, the two work on different principles:
§bDrill:§/b Rotates, cuts, and abrades
§bUltrasonic Tip:§/b Does not rotate or cut; it vibrates at a high frequency
How the Procedure Works:
§bVibration:§/b The metal tip of the instrument vibrates at a high frequency and, when it touches the tartar, creates a shock wave that "breaks up" the tartar
§bWater (Cavitation):§/b Pressurized water both cools the heat and flushes away the broken-up tartar
§bResult:§/b These vibrations are tuned to break up tartar. When used with the correct technique, they are not expected to harm the enamel, the hardest tissue in the body.
Other Myths and Honest Answers
1. "My Teeth Became Very Sensitive After Cleaning"
§bHonest Answer:§/b This usually does not mean the enamel was scratched. Sensitivity lasting 1-2 days after the treatment is common.

§bWhy:§/b The root surfaces of your teeth had been covered for months by a thick "blanket of tartar". This blanket "insulated" your tooth against cold. When we lift that blanket, the clean root surface meets external stimuli for the first time.
This temporary sensitivity is a sign not that your tooth has been "damaged" but that it has been §b"cleaned"§/b.
2. "Tartar Removal Opened the Spaces Between My Teeth (Black Triangles)"
§bHonest Answer:§/b The ultrasonic instrument does not "wear away" that area; it "cleans" it.
§bWhy:§/b In most cases the "gap" you see was already there and reflects bone loss caused by periodontitis.
§bWhy Do You See It Now?§/b Because that gap had been "camouflaged" by two things:
The tartar itself filling that gap
The gum swollen by the infection the tartar caused
When we remove the tartar, the gum heals and shrinks. Once both the tartar and the swelling are gone, the bone loss that the disease had already caused becomes visible.
3. "My Teeth Wobble More After Cleaning"
§bHonest Answer:§/b In this situation the teeth have usually already lost their bone support because of periodontitis and started to wobble.
§bFalse Support:§/b The heavy tartar around the teeth had "glued" those wobbly teeth together, creating false support.

When we clean away that false "concrete", the teeth were freed, and the real looseness that the disease had already caused came to light. §bCleaning does not usually cause looseness; it reveals looseness that is already there.§/b
4. "My Teeth Get Dirty Faster After Cleaning"
§bPolishing:§/b After scaling, the "polishing" step is important. The tooth surfaces are made smooth with a special polishing paste and a rotating brush.
§bResult:§/b It is harder for bacterial plaque to reattach to a smooth surface.
Why Is It Harmful Not to Have Tartar Removed?
Tartar is not a "dead" layer of limescale but §b"a living nest of bacteria"§/b.
Risks:
§bGingivitis:§/b Constantly bleeding, swollen, red gums
§bPeriodontitis:§/b Bone loss, gum recession, looseness
§bTooth Loss:§/b Teeth that lose their bone support may be lost over time
§bGeneral Health:§/b Gum diseases have been associated with conditions such as cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and pregnancy complications
Conclusion: The Importance of Preventive Care
Tartar formation is a lifelong process. Tartar removal is §ba preventive care§/b done at intervals your dentist recommends according to your situation (generally every 6 months for most people).
Regular check-ups and cleanings may help reduce the risk of needing more extensive treatments later.
§bAbout the Author:§/b This article was written and medically reviewed by §bDr. Emrecan Eren§/b. Our clinic provides care to its patients with evidence-based treatment protocols.

fissur-ortucu-dis-asisi.title: What Is a Fissure Sealant (Tooth Vaccine)? A Procedure That Protects Molars From Cavities
fissur-ortucu-dis-asisi.lead: A protective procedure that seals the deep grooves in molars.

b.x: As a parent, you do everything you can to protect your child's health. You have them vaccinated to protect them from diseases. But did you know there is also a "vaccine" to protect your child's teeth, the permanent teeth they will use for a lifetime, from this common and contagious disease called §b"tooth decay"§/b?

The fissure sealant, known as the §b"Tooth Vaccine"§/b, takes on exactly this role. It is not a real vaccine involving an injection, but it is called by this nickname because of its protective purpose.
The Real Problem: What Is a "Fissure" and Why Is the Brush Not Enough?
To understand why a fissure sealant is "needed", we first need to know where our enemy (decay) hides.
The Problem: The Anatomy of Our Molars

Take a close look at the chewing surfaces of your child's back molars. These surfaces are not flat; they are full of "cusps" and §b"grooves"§/b. These deep, narrow grooves and pits are called §b"Fissures"§/b.
The Brush Falls Short

These fissures are so narrow and deep that the bristles of a toothbrush physically cannot reach the bottom of the groove. While the bristle cleans the surface of the groove, food debris and bacteria get trapped at the bottom of it.
§bGood to Know:§/b Cavities in children often start on these chewing surfaces of the teeth called "fissures".
How Does a Fissure Sealant Work? (The Protective Shield)
A fissure sealant is a "biocompatible" and fluid-consistency §b"protective coating"§/b material. It is generally a resin-based material in a tooth color (white or clear).
Protection Mechanism:
§bCleaning:§/b The tooth surface is thoroughly cleaned of the fissures
§bFluid Application:§/b The liquid "protective coating" is applied to the chewing surface of the tooth. It seeps all the way down into the deepest grooves
§bSealing:§/b It is hardened with a special blue (LED) light
§bResult:§/b A rough, grooved surface → becomes a smooth, slick, "cleanable" surface
§bAnalogy:§/b It is like sealing the grout between the tiles in your bathroom with a waterproof coating. You seal the grout and prevent mold from forming.
Does It Really Work?

A fissure sealant is a widely used preventive procedure that helps reduce the risk of cavities on the chewing surfaces of molars. For its protective effect, it is important that the sealant stays in place and intact; for this reason it is monitored at regular check-ups.
Step by Step: Will It Hurt My Child?

§bHow It Is Applied:§/b This procedure usually does not require an injection (anesthesia) or drilling. After the tooth surface is cleaned and dried, the sealant is applied and hardened with light; it takes a few minutes per tooth.
4 Simple Steps:
§bExamination and Cleaning:§/b The tooth surface is cleaned with a special brush and paste
§bSurface Preparation:§/b A gentle solution is applied for 15-20 seconds (it does not harm the tooth)
§bApplication:§/b The fluid fissure sealant is applied with a brush "as if painting"
§bHardening:§/b The blue LED light is held for 20-30 seconds and the material turns into "a hard shield"
§bDone!§/b Since the procedure usually does not require anesthesia, there is no numbness, and in most cases the child can eat right away.
Frequently Asked Questions
1. Which Teeth, and When Should It Be Done?
§bKey Target: 6-Year Molars:§/b The first permanent molar erupts at about age 6. It should be applied as soon as it comes in (within the first 6 months)
§bSecond Target: 12-Year Molars:§/b The second permanent molars are at the same risk
§bBaby Teeth:§/b If needed, it can also be applied to baby molars
2. Is It Safe? Does It Contain Harmful Substances (BPA)?
§bMaterial:§/b Fissure sealants are materials that have been used in dentistry for a long time. You can talk to your dentist about the contents of the material used and your questions about BPA.
3. Does It Last a Lifetime?
§bDurability:§/b Fissure sealants can wear down over time; how long they last varies from person to person.
§bCheck-up:§/b We check its condition at our routine check-ups. If there is wear, it can usually be renewed with a short procedure.
4. Can They Stop Brushing Their Teeth Now?
§bNo.§/b A fissure sealant only protects the grooves on the chewing surface of the tooth; it does not protect the sides of the teeth.
§bComprehensive Protection:§/b Fissure Sealant + Fluoride Application + Good Brushing = More Comprehensive Protection
Conclusion: Cavities Are Not "Treated", They Are "Prevented"
Our priority is to prevent decay §bbefore a filling or root canal treatment is needed§/b.
Taking your child's 6-year molars under protection before decay forms is an important part of preventive dentistry.
The Fissure Sealant (Tooth Vaccine) is a simple preventive procedure applied for this purpose, and it usually does not require anesthesia.
§bAbout the Author:§/b This article was written and medically reviewed by §bDr. Emrecan Eren§/b. Our clinic provides care to its patients with evidence-based treatment protocols.

florur-uygulamasi-cocuklar.title: Fluoride Treatment: Is It Safe and Necessary for Children? The Scientific Facts
florur-uygulamasi-cocuklar.lead: Myth vs. fact: the safety and effectiveness of topical fluoride.

b.x: As a parent, it is completely normal to feel confused when making a decision about your child's health, especially when there is so much conflicting information online. On one side are worrying headlines saying "fluoride is poison"; on the other, your dentist's advice that "fluoride is essential for your child's dental health."

§bQuick answer:§/b Yes. "Topical" fluoride, applied at the right dose and under the supervision of a professional dentist, is one of the widely used, minimally invasive preventive methods that help protect your child against tooth decay.
What Exactly Is Fluoride? (Not a "Poison" but a "Mineral")

Let's correct the myth first: §bFluoride is not a synthetic "poison" made in a laboratory.§/b Like calcium, magnesium, or phosphorus, fluoride is a mineral found naturally in nature (in the earth's crust, rocks, soil, and drinking water).
It is found naturally in many foods: tea, fish, spinach... The fluoride we use in dentistry is a "purified" and "dosed" form of this natural mineral.
You can think of it as a §b"vitamin"§/b or "mineral supplement" for our teeth. Just as vitamin D strengthens our bones, fluoride strengthens our teeth.
How Does Fluoride Protect the Tooth? (3 Mechanisms)
1. It Forms "Super Enamel" (Fluorapatite)
The natural enamel of our teeth is made of "Hydroxyapatite" crystals. This structure is strong but "sensitive" to acid.
When fluoride comes into contact with the tooth surface, it converts this structure into a crystal structure called §b"Fluorapatite"§/b, which is more resistant to acid.
§bSteel Vest Analogy:§/b If tooth enamel is normally a "bulletproof vest", fluoride-strengthened enamel is like a "steel vest". It becomes more resistant to acid attacks.
2. It Performs "Remineralization" (Repair)
Fluoride is not a "passive" shield; it is an "active" repair crew. When an acid attack begins, fluoride captures calcium and phosphate minerals in the saliva and "repairs" the damaged areas.
3. It Has an Antibacterial Effect
Fluoride disrupts the metabolism of bacteria. It slows the growth of acid-producing bacteria and reduces their capacity to produce acid.
The Biggest Concern: "Is Fluoride Toxic?" (Myth vs. Fact)
We understand this concern and take it very seriously. §bAnswer:§/b As with everything, the main factor that determines whether it is harmful is §bthe dose§/b.
The Scientific Principle:
Water is life. But drinking too much water in a short time can be harmful
Vitamin A is necessary for eye health, but an excessive dose can damage the liver
Fluoride is the same way. At extremely high doses it can be harmful
An Important Distinction: "Topical" vs. "Systemic"
Most of the concerns online are about the risks of "high doses" of "systemic" (ingested) fluoride.
§bSystemic (Ingested):§/b Fluoride the child swallows, which enters the bloodstream (drops, tablets)
§bTopical (Surface - Applied at Our Clinic):§/b A "varnish" or "gel" that the child does not swallow, applied only to the outer surface of the tooth
§bIts Purpose:§/b Not to enter the bloodstream. Only to stay on the tooth surface for 4-6 hours and form the "Super Enamel".
General Approach:
Professional topical fluoride application is §bone of the widely recommended preventive methods§/b in dentistry for protection against decay.
"We Had a Fissure Sealant Done. Is Fluoride Still Necessary?"
§bAnswer: In most cases, yes.§/b These two treatments are not "rivals" but a "team" that "complements" each other.
§bFissure Sealant:§/b Mechanically seals the "pits" of the molars. Protects only the chewing surface
§bFluoride Application:§/b Chemically strengthens the "smooth surfaces" and the "contact surfaces between teeth"

§bConclusion:§/b The fissure sealant protects the "pit", and fluoride protects the "flat surface" and the "contact surface". For more comprehensive protection, your dentist may recommend both together.
How Is the Procedure Done at Our Clinic?
No needle, anesthesia, or "drill" is used in the procedure.
4 Simple Steps:
§bExamination and Cleaning:§/b The tooth surfaces are cleaned with professional paste and a brush
§bDrying:§/b The tooth surfaces are gently dried with air
§bVarnish Application:§/b The fluoride varnish (usually strawberry or bubblegum flavored) is applied with a small brush "like nail polish"
§bInstant Setting:§/b The varnish hardens the moment it touches saliva and adheres to the tooth surface
§bDone!§/b The whole procedure takes 1-2 minutes.
Post-Procedure Instructions:
§bEating and Drinking:§/b Not eating or drinking anything for 30 minutes to 1 hour
§bHard Foods:§/b Avoiding very hot, hard, or sticky foods that day (4-6 hours)
§bBrushing:§/b Usually no brushing that day (in the evening). Return to the normal routine the next morning
§bFrequency:§/b Repeated every 6 months or every 3-4 months, depending on the cavity risk
Conclusion: A Decision Based on Knowledge
As a parent, it is important to decide by talking with your dentist about your child's situation rather than relying on conflicting information online.
Fluoride application, together with a Fissure Sealant, is a simple §bpreventive procedure§/b that helps protect your child's permanent teeth.
§bAbout the Author:§/b This article was written and medically reviewed by §bDr. Emrecan Eren§/b. Our clinic provides care to its patients with evidence-based treatment protocols.

gulus-tasarimi-temel-ilkeler.title: Is "Smile Design" Only About Aesthetics? The 3 Basic Principles of a Healthy Smile
gulus-tasarimi-temel-ilkeler.lead: Gum health, jaw function, and the importance of a holistic approach.

b.x: The term "smile design" has become one of the most popular expressions in aesthetic dentistry in recent years. But this popularity has also brought a misconception: many patients see smile design as only "whitening" or "veneering" the teeth. In fact, this is §bonly the visible tip of the iceberg§/b.
At our clinic, we look at smile design with a holistic approach. For us, a good smile should not only be aesthetically pleasing but also §bhealthy, functional, and sustainable§/b.
§bThe risk of problems may increase in aesthetic procedures (laminate veneers, zirconia) done without a solid foundation (health and function).§/b
Principle 1: Health and Function
This is our first step before starting any aesthetic procedure. §bAesthetics is built on top of health.§/b
Healthy Gums First: "Pink Aesthetics"

Even a carefully made porcelain veneer may not give the desired result when placed on swollen, red, bleeding, and asymmetrical gums. A beautiful painting only makes sense with a beautiful frame (healthy gums).
"Gummy Smile":
If your gums show too much when you smile (Gummy Smile), then in suitable cases adjusting the gum levels with a small surgical or laser procedure called §b"Gingivectomy"§/b may be considered.
Periodontal Health:

If there is gum inflammation (gingivitis) or more advanced gum disease (periodontitis), all aesthetic procedures are paused. Gum treatment (Periodontology) is performed first, and tartar (scaling) and inflamed tissues (curettage) are cleaned.
§b"Pink aesthetics" is the foundation of white aesthetics.§/b Healthy, pale pink, and symmetrical gums directly affect the success and natural look of the restoration to be made.
Correct Bite (Occlusion) and Chewing Function
Your smile is not just a "showcase"; it is part of a complex chewing system (the stomatognathic system).
Faulty Bite:

If your teeth do not close properly (malocclusion), newly made porcelain veneers or zirconia crowns may be subjected to excessive and uneven load. This can increase the risk of the restorations breaking or cracking.
Bruxism (Teeth Clenching):
Many patients are unaware that they clench their teeth at night (Bruxism). This habit can lead to fractures in ceramic restorations.
Our Approach:

Before starting digital smile design, we evaluate your bite in detail. If needed, we plan either to correct the position of the teeth first with orthodontic treatment (clear aligners) or to bring these forces under control with treatment for clenching (bruxism) (for example, a night guard).
Biocompatibility: Tissue-Friendly Materials

Material selection is another health aspect of aesthetics. It is important that the material used is compatible with the tissues. In suitable cases, choosing zirconia or all-ceramic materials instead of metal-supported porcelain can help prevent the dark line that can be visible at the gum margin.
Principle 2: Aesthetic Proportion and Harmony
After laying a solid foundation, the aesthetic planning stage begins. A natural smile should be in harmony with your facial proportions and the character of your face.
Facial Symmetry and the Midline

Our first reference point in smile design is the midline of your face. The vertical line assumed to pass through the middle of your two pupils and the tip of your nose should ideally pass through the point where your two upper front teeth meet. Millimeter deviations from this line are natural, but preserving this line is critical for the perception of a symmetrical smile.
Smile Arc: Dynamic Aesthetics
This is one of the important aesthetic criteria. When you smile, the curve formed by the biting edges of your upper front teeth should follow the curve of your lower lip in parallel.
§bYoung and Attractive Smile:§/b When the upper teeth follow the lower lip (a convex line), this is perceived as a dynamic and youthful smile.
§bOlder or Tired Smile:§/b If this line is flattened or reversed (concave), it creates a tired and older expression.
Tooth Shape and Proportions
Your teeth reflect your character. The same tooth shape is not applied to everyone.
Proportions:
The proportions between the widths of the front teeth play a role in how balanced the smile is perceived. These proportions are evaluated individually.
Shape Selection:

Your face shape guides the choice of tooth shape. For example, while more angular and pronounced tooth shapes can suit square facial features, rounder tooth shapes with softer corners can suit oval facial features. The length and width of the teeth should be proportionate to the overall dimensions of your face.
Principle 3: Digital Planning
This last principle involves supporting aesthetic planning with digital tools.
Why 3D Scanning and Digital Smile Design?
Smile design can also be planned with wax-ups on plaster models. Digital methods, on the other hand, allow the plan to be reviewed with the patient on screen.
At our clinic, we manage the process as follows:
With intraoral 3D scanners, we create a digital, three-dimensional model of your teeth; in many cases this reduces the need for traditional impression trays.
We take photographs of your face.
We combine these two sets of data in smile design software.
"Mock-Up" (Trial): Seeing the Plan Before It Begins
Digital design helps you §bvisualize§/b the planned result before treatment begins.
Digital Simulation:
On the computer screen, we simulate for you how your new smile would look on your face, with different color and shape options.
Physical Trial (Mock-Up):
After we agree on the design, it is produced on a 3D printer. The resulting temporary template is placed in your mouth without any work on your teeth.
Trial:

When you look in the mirror, you see a temporary trial (mock-up) of the planned design in your mouth. At this stage, we make final touches based on your feedback, such as "I wish my teeth were a little longer" or "I really like the color".

Seeing the plan before any irreversible procedure (such as reshaping) is done on your teeth helps §bclarify expectations§/b. The trial may not be exactly the same as the final result; the final result may differ depending on the person's tooth and gum structure.
Conclusion: Smile Design Is Teamwork

As you can see, smile design is a §bholistic§/b process that extends from gum health to facial proportions and digital planning. It is not something done by the dentist alone; it is teamwork in which the patient's expectations are heard, the dentist makes the clinical assessment, and dental technicians contribute.

At our clinic in Lüleburgaz, we work to combine these three principles to design a smile for you that is not only "aesthetic" but also §b"healthy" and "functional"§/b and, most importantly, §b"personal to you"§/b.
§bAbout the Author:§/b This article was written and medically reviewed by §bDr. Emrecan Eren§/b. Our clinic provides care to its patients with evidence-based treatment protocols.

hamilelikte-dis-tedavisi.title: Is Dental Treatment Safe During Pregnancy?
hamilelikte-dis-tedavisi.lead: Oral health during pregnancy, safe treatment periods and points to keep in mind.

b.x: Pregnancy is not a reason to neglect oral health; on the contrary, hormonal changes can make gum problems more likely. Postponing a problem that needs treatment, on the other hand, can create a risk of pain and infection for the mother. For this reason, dental examinations and necessary treatments during pregnancy are planned in coordination with your obstetrician.
What Changes in the Mouth During Pregnancy?
§bPregnancy gingivitis:§/b Redness, swelling and bleeding while brushing are common in the gums.
§bNausea and vomiting:§/b Stomach acid can affect the enamel.
§bChanges in eating habits:§/b Frequent snacking and sweet cravings can increase the risk of cavities.
Which Period Is Suitable for Treatment?

For treatments that can be planned, the §bsecond trimester§/b (about months 4–6) is generally considered the most comfortable period. Urgent problems such as pain, swelling or infection are treated at any stage of pregnancy, with the necessary precautions. Cosmetic procedures and whitening are usually left until after birth.
X-rays and Anesthesia
§bX-rays:§/b When truly necessary, a low-dose dental X-ray can be taken with a protective apron. Unnecessary imaging is not done.
§bLocal anesthesia:§/b Local anesthetics used in dental treatment can be used during pregnancy at an appropriate dose. Numbing is preferred over being treated while in pain.
§bMedications:§/b When a pain reliever or antibiotic is needed, medications suitable for use during pregnancy are chosen. Do not take medication on your own.
When You Come for an Appointment
Tell your dentist how many weeks pregnant you are and which medications you take.
Lying on your back for a long time may be uncomfortable; let us know when you would like a break.
Share any special warnings from your obstetrician.
Home Care
Brush twice a day with a fluoride toothpaste and a soft brush; clean between your teeth.
After vomiting, rinse your mouth with water instead of brushing right away.
If gum bleeding increases, come in for an examination and tartar cleaning.
Conclusion
Dental treatment during pregnancy can be done at the right time and with the necessary precautions. If you have gum bleeding, pain or swelling, we recommend contacting your dentist without waiting.
This content is for general information only; for diagnosis and treatment, please consult your dentist and your obstetrician.

hareketli-protez-alisma-sureci.title: Getting Used to a Removable Denture: Tips and Recommendations
hareketli-protez-alisma-sureci.lead: The adjustment timeline, managing sore spots and practical tips.

b.x: You have received your new removable denture. Perhaps, after years, you are excited to have a full smile and chewing function again. But when you first put your denture in, what you feel may be less "excitement" and more §b"strangeness."§/b
We want to start with the most honest truth: §bIn most cases, these feelings are normal.§/b Getting used to a new denture is not a single "event"; it is a "process."
Why Does It Feel So "Foreign"?
For decades, your brain has memorized the map inside your mouth. A new denture changes that memorized map all at once.
Main Challenges During the Adjustment Period:
§b"Foreign Object" Feeling:§/b Your brain perceives the denture as "food" or a "foreign object." Its first reaction is to "throw it out" (nausea) or to "digest it" (excess saliva).
§bMuscle Memory:§/b Your tongue, lips and cheek muscles have to learn again how to adapt to this new surface.
§bSpeech:§/b Your tongue touches your palate thousands of times a day to form sounds such as "S," "SH" and "T." Now the acrylic surface of the denture is there.
§bChange in Bite:§/b Your new denture is designed according to the ideal closing position of your jaw. Even this "correct" position can feel "wrong" at first.
Adjustment Timeline: A 4-Week Process
Stage 1: The First 24–48 Hours ("Shock and Discovery")
§bWhat You Will Feel:§/b Excess saliva, mild nausea, a "lisp" in speech and whistling on "s" sounds.
§bWhat to Do:§/b Be patient and do not take your denture out. Your brain needs to be "exposed" to it in order to adjust.
Stage 2: The First Week (the "Sore Spot" Period)
§bWhat You Will Feel:§/b This is the most challenging week. Some "hard" spots on your denture may begin to cause sores on your gums. These are called "sore spots."
§bWhat to Do:§/b These "sore spots" are normal. Do not try to adjust the denture yourself.
Stage 3: Weeks 2–4 ("The New Normal")
§bWhat You Will Feel:§/b You have gone to your dentist for the "sore spots" and adjustments have been made. You generally feel more comfortable, and your speech improves noticeably.
Stage 4: After 1 Month ("Autopilot")
§bWhat You Will Feel:§/b Most people "think" about their denture less during this period. Muscle memory has started to adapt to the new situation.
The Most Important Obstacle: Managing "Sore Spots" (Pain/Sores)
Just as a new pair of shoes can rub your foot, your new denture will rub your gums. This is unavoidable and normal.
What You Should Do:
§bMake an Appointment:§/b A check-up appointment within 24–48 hours of receiving the denture
§bBefore the Appointment:§/b Be sure to wear your denture for at least 4–6 hours beforehand (the sore area needs to be red)
§bAdjustment:§/b Your dentist grinds away a tiny amount, measured in millimeters, from the inner surface at that red spot
What You Should Not Do:
§bSanding the Denture:§/b Grinding it down yourself at home with a file upsets the balance of the denture
§bLeaving the Denture in a Drawer:§/b If you do not wear it because "it hurts," the adjustment process becomes harder; contact your dentist instead
Speaking Guide for Denture Wearers
It is normal for your speech to change. Your tongue needs to get used to touching the new "palate" surface.
3 Practical Tips:
§bRead Aloud:§/b Read a newspaper or book for 15 minutes every day
§bSlow Down and Repeat:§/b Slowly repeat the words you find difficult (such as "Sunshine" or "Seashell")
§bSing:§/b Singing in the shower or in the car is a great exercise for the tongue muscles
Eating Guide for Denture Wearers
Start Soft (First Week):
Start with foods that do not require chewing, such as soup, yogurt, purée, boiled vegetables and soft-boiled eggs.
Practical Tip: Chew on Both Sides
Divide the food in two and place it over both your right and left back teeth at the same time, chewing on both sides. This helps your denture stay balanced and not tip over.
Avoid Biting with the Front Teeth
Do not try to bite off an apple or a sandwich with your front teeth while wearing a denture. Cut food with a knife and chew it with your back teeth.
Denture Care and Hygiene
Take Your Denture Out at Night (Important Rule)
§bWhy?§/b Your gums need to rest. Sleeping with a denture can increase the risk of a fungal infection.
§bWhat to Do:§/b Take the denture out, brush it, and store it in a special container (in water).
How Should It Be Cleaned?
§bDo Not Use Toothpaste:§/b Abrasive particles scratch the denture
§bThe Right Method:§/b Use a denture brush and a non-abrasive denture paste
§bEffervescent Tablets:§/b A few times a week, soak it in water containing special cleaning tablets
Conclusion: Patience, Communication and Follow-Up

Getting used to a removable denture is like learning to ride a bicycle again. It may feel unsteady and awkward at first. In most cases, however, your muscles, tongue and brain adapt to this new situation over time.

Every "sore spot" or worry you have is a normal part of this process. Do not feel alone, and do not leave your denture in a drawer. Call us. Making those tiny adjustments and managing this process together is our job.
§bAbout the Author:§/b This article was written and medically reviewed by §bDr. Emrecan Eren§/b. Our clinic provides care based on evidence-based treatment protocols.

implant-acitir-mi.title: Does a Dental Implant Hurt? What to Expect During Surgery and Recovery
implant-acitir-mi.lead: What you need to know about anesthesia, pain management and the healing process.

b.x: Does Implant Treatment Hurt?

One of the most frequently asked questions about implant treatment is "Does it hurt?" The short answer: §bThe aim is that no pain is felt during the procedure, thanks to local anesthesia.§/b Most patients feel only pressure, rather than pain, during surgery.
During the Procedure: Local Anesthesia
Implant surgery is performed under §blocal anesthesia§/b. This means that the area to be treated is numbed. While the anesthesia is working:
The aim is that no pain is felt
You may feel pressure and touch (not pain)
You are fully awake and conscious
You can communicate with your dentist
Options for Anxiety
For patients with a high level of dental anxiety, the following options can be discussed with your dentist in addition to local anesthesia:
§bSedation:§/b Mild calming medication
§bConscious sedation:§/b Deeper relaxation
§bGeneral anesthesia:§/b In very rare cases, for complex situations
After the Procedure: The First 24–48 Hours
Once the anesthesia wears off (after 2–4 hours), mild to moderate discomfort is normal:
Expected Symptoms:
§bMild pain:§/b Can usually be controlled with pain relievers
§bSwelling:§/b Peaks within 2–3 days, then decreases
§bTenderness:§/b Sensitivity to touch around the implant area
§bMild bleeding:§/b Minimal bleeding may occur within the first 24 hours
Pain Management:
Your dentist will give you a pain management plan:
§bPain relievers:§/b The medication and dose your dentist considers suitable for you
§bPrescription medication:§/b If needed, after your dentist's evaluation
§bIce pack:§/b To reduce swelling during the first 24 hours
Healing Process: The First Week
Most patients can return to their normal activities 3–5 days after the procedure:
§bDays 1–3:§/b The most discomfort, pain reliever use
§bDays 4–7:§/b Swelling and pain decrease noticeably
§bDays 7–10:§/b Stitches are removed (if they were used)
Long-Term Healing: Osseointegration
The fusion of the implant with the bone (osseointegration) usually takes a few months; the duration varies from person to person. During this period:
Pain is not usually expected; if you do have pain, contact your dentist
You can continue your normal daily activities
Regular check-ups are important
Warning Signs: When Should You See a Dentist?
The following symptoms are not normal, and you should contact your dentist:
Severe or increasing pain despite pain relievers
High fever (above 38°C)
Excessive swelling or redness
Pus discharge from the implant area
The implant feeling loose
Implant vs. Tooth Extraction: Comparing Pain
The discomfort felt after implant surgery varies depending on the person and the extent of the case; some patients describe it as similar to a tooth extraction. Factors that affect discomfort:
The procedure being controlled and planned
Keeping trauma to the tissues limited
Whether an additional procedure (bone graft, sinus lift, etc.) is needed
Following the instructions given after the procedure
Conclusion

In implant treatment, §bpatient comfort is taken into account§/b through local anesthesia and pain management. The aim is that no pain is felt during the procedure; discomfort after the procedure can in most cases be managed with pain relievers.
At §bDr. Emrecan Eren Clinic§/b, we regard patient comfort as a priority. You can make an appointment for detailed information and a personalized treatment plan.
