implant-mi-kopru-mu.title: Implant or Bridge for a Missing Tooth?
implant-mi-kopru-mu.lead: How the two methods are done, how they differ and what is considered when deciding.

b.x: Leaving the space of an extracted or lost tooth empty can cause neighboring teeth to tilt toward the gap, the opposing tooth to grow longer (over-erupt) and the bite to be disrupted. Two of the most commonly used fixed treatment options are the §bimplant§/b and the §bbridge§/b. Which one is suitable is decided together at the examination, based on the condition of the mouth.
How Is a Bridge Made?

In a bridge, the teeth on both sides of the gap are reduced in size and prepared for crowns, and the missing tooth is cemented in as a single piece attached to these two teeth. It does not require surgery and is usually completed within a few weeks.
How Is an Implant Made?

In an implant, a titanium screw is placed in the jawbone where the tooth is missing. You usually wait a few months for the screw to fuse with the bone; then a crown is made on top. No work is done on the neighboring teeth. If there is not enough bone, additional bone procedures may be needed.
Comparison
§bNeighboring teeth:§/b In a bridge, the neighboring teeth are reduced in size; with an implant, the neighboring teeth are not touched.
§bTime:§/b A bridge is usually completed in a shorter time; an implant requires a period for fusion with the bone.
§bSurgery:§/b A bridge does not require surgery; an implant is a minor surgical procedure.
§bBone:§/b An implant transmits load to the bone where it is placed, which helps preserve the bone; the bone in the space under a bridge may shrink over time.
§bCleaning:§/b The underside of a bridge needs to be cleaned with special floss or an interdental brush; an implant crown is brushed and flossed like a natural tooth.
What Is Considered When Deciding?
Whether the neighboring teeth already have large fillings or crowns
The amount and quality of the bone in the area (evaluated with a CT scan)
General health, smoking and the medications used
Gum health
The patient's expectations and preference regarding treatment time

For example, if the neighboring teeth are healthy and have no fillings, an implant may be considered so that they do not have to be reduced. If the neighboring teeth already need crowns, a bridge may be a reasonable option.
Conclusion

The implant and the bridge are two established methods used to replace a missing tooth with a fixed restoration. Which one is suitable is decided together with your dentist after the neighboring teeth, the bone and your general health have been evaluated.
This content is for general information only; for diagnosis and treatment, please consult your dentist.

implant-sonrasi-beslenme.title: Nutrition Guide After Implant Treatment: What to Eat in the First Week
implant-sonrasi-beslenme.lead: Eating recommendations during healing and what to avoid.

b.x: You have completed your implant surgery. An implant has been placed in the space of your missing tooth. Now it is your turn: the §bhealing process§/b.
After surgery, especially during the first week, your diet is one of the important factors that directly affect the outcome of this treatment and your comfort.
The Basis of Healing: What Is Osseointegration?

To understand why nutrition after an implant matters so much, it helps to know how an implant works. After the implant is placed in the jawbone, bone cells (osteoblasts) grow toward the titanium surface of the implant and join with it biologically. This process is called §b"osseointegration"§/b.

This is the process that allows the implant to function like a "tooth root." It usually takes 3 to 6 months. However, the §bfirst week§/b is the period in which this biological bonding is most delicate, the wound is closing and the risk of infection is highest.
The First 24–48 Hours: The "Cold, Liquid and Passive" Period

This is the most restrictive but most important period of the whole process, the calm before the storm. Your body tries to give "first aid" by forming a blood clot in the area. Our job is to protect this clot.
Rule 1: Do Not Drink Anything Hot
For the first 24 hours after surgery, hot coffee, hot tea or hot soup should not be consumed.

§bScientific Reason:§/b Heat causes "vasodilation," that is, widening of the blood vessels. This can trigger bleeding in the surgical area, increase swelling (edema) and disturb the blood clot, which is the cornerstone of healing.
§bWhat to Do:§/b All liquids should be cold or at room temperature. Cold narrows the blood vessels (vasoconstriction), reduces bleeding and naturally numbs the area.
Rule 2: Avoid Sucking and Spitting Movements
This rule is meant to prevent the risk of "dry socket" (alveolar osteitis, inflammation of the extraction site), which can negatively affect your healing.
§bDo Not Use a Straw:§/b Drinking through a straw creates negative pressure in the mouth and can "suck" the blood clot out of place.
§bDo Not Smoke:§/b Smoking is also a sucking movement and disturbs the clot. In addition, smoke narrows the blood vessels that support healing and may increase the risk of implant failure.
§bDo Not Spit or Swish:§/b Simply swallow the liquid in your mouth. Forceful spitting or swishing can also dislodge the clot.
First 48 Hours Food List (Liquid/Cold)
§bDrinks:§/b Cold water, milk at room temperature, cold ayran (a yogurt drink), strained compote juices (non-acidic, e.g., apple).
§bSoups (Cold/Lukewarm):§/b Blended, smooth, cold soups (e.g., cold yogurt soup, strained vegetable soup).
§bDairy Products:§/b Plain yogurt, kefir (smooth), rice pudding (with the rice mashed), milk pudding.
§bBonus:§/b Sugar-free ice cream. Its cold effect numbs the area and reduces swelling.
Day 3 to Day 7: The "Soft Purée" Period

Congratulations, you have gotten through the hardest 48 hours. The wound has started to close and the clot has stabilized. We can now begin giving your body "healing fuel" (protein and vitamins), but §bno chewing should be done on the surgical site§/b yet.
Permitted Soft Foods (Focused on Protein and Vitamins)
§bSoups (Warm):§/b You can now drink them warm. Blended lentil, broccoli and zucchini soups.
§bEggs:§/b Scrambled or soft-boiled eggs are a good source of protein for healing.
§bPotatoes:§/b Boiled or baked mashed potatoes (should not be too hot).
§bVegetables:§/b Boiled and puréed vegetables (zucchini, carrots, peas).
§bFish:§/b Very well-cooked, boneless, soft white fish (salmon, whiting).
§bOthers:§/b Mashed avocado, hummus, aged cheeses, well-cooked pasta.
What to Avoid During the First Week
1. Hard Foods (Mechanical Risk)
§bNot allowed:§/b Nuts (hazelnuts, walnuts), chips, popcorn, crusty bread, simit (sesame bread ring), cookies.
§bWhy:§/b These foods can press on the implant or the stitches, cause pain and negatively affect the osseointegration of the implant.
2. Small and Grainy Foods (Infection Risk)
§bNot allowed:§/b Sesame (on simit), bulgur (in pilaf), quinoa, strawberry/kiwi seeds, black peppercorns.
§bWhy:§/b These small particles can slip into the wound area or between the stitches and lead to infections that are hard to notice.
3. Sticky Foods (Mechanical Risk)
§bNot allowed:§/b Chewing gum, Turkish delight, caramel candies.
§bWhy:§/b They can stick to the stitches or to the temporary healing cap on the implant and move them out of place.
4. Acidic and Spicy Foods (Chemical Irritation)
§bNot allowed:§/b Hot pepper, very spicy foods, lemon, orange juice, vinegar, pickles.
§bWhy:§/b These foods chemically "burn" (irritate) the surgical area, which is an open wound, and delay healing.
5. Alcohol and Smoking (Biological Risk)
§bSmoking:§/b Narrows the capillaries that support healing, reduces oxygen supply to the area and may negatively affect the osseointegration of the implant.
§bAlcohol:§/b Slows the healing process, causes dehydration and can interact dangerously with your prescription pain relievers. It is recommended to stay away from it during the first week.
When Will I Return to Normal Food? (Healing Timeline)
§bWeek 1 (Until the Stitches Are Removed):§/b Stick to the "Liquid & Purée" diet above. It is recommended not to chew on the surgical site.
§bWeeks 2–4:§/b After the stitches are removed and the wound has closed, you slowly move from "soft" foods to "normal" foods.
§bMonth 3 and Beyond:§/b The fusion of your implant with the bone (osseointegration) is still continuing. Continue to avoid hard foods.

§bFinal Stage (After the Permanent Restoration Is Placed):§/b Usually after 3–6 months, once your implant has joined with the bone and Dr. Eren has placed your permanent restoration on it, you can return to a normal diet in line with your dentist's recommendations.
Conclusion: Patience and Care for Healthy Healing

Implant treatment requires careful planning and surgical precision. At our clinic, we aim to make this process as comfortable as possible with 3D digital planning and a minimally invasive surgical approach. However, §bthe care you take during the first week§/b also plays an important role in healing.
Following this nutrition guide is one of the first steps you can take to help your implant stay healthy for a long time.
§bAbout the Author:§/b This article was written and medically reviewed by §bDr. Emrecan Eren§/b. Our clinic provides care based on evidence-based treatment protocols.

kanal-tedavisi-sonrasi-agri.title: Is Pain After Root Canal Treatment Normal? Healing and Warning Signs
kanal-tedavisi-sonrasi-agri.lead: The differences between normal tenderness and signs of infection.

b.x: Root canal treatment is performed to save a tooth that "might otherwise have to be extracted." Perhaps you have just had this treatment and feel some tenderness or an ache in your tooth. We know the critical question on your mind: §b"Is this pain normal, or is something going wrong?"§/b
§bQuick answer:§/b Yes, feeling mild tenderness or an ache during the first few days after treatment is generally normal and expected.
If the Nerve Was Removed, Why Does It Still Hurt? (Scientific Explanation)

This is the most logical question our patients ask. "If the nerve (pulp) of the tooth has been completely cleaned out, there shouldn't be anything left to feel pain, right?" This is sound reasoning, but it is incomplete information.

Root canal treatment cleans the infected nerve tissue inside the tooth. But this procedure is, in essence, a §b"micro-surgical"§/b operation. The cause of the pain is no longer the "inside" of the tooth but its §b"surroundings."§/b
Inflammation of the Surrounding Tissues:

The tooth sits in a "socket" (alveolus) in the jawbone and is attached to this socket by microscopic fibers called the "periodontal ligament." During treatment, the instruments (files) and disinfectant solutions used to clean the root tip cause a temporary, small reaction (inflammation) in the tissues beyond the root tip where these fibers are located. This is the body's natural healing response.
Pressure from the Temporary Filling:

Between or at the end of root canal appointments, a temporary (or permanent) filling is placed on the tooth. This filling can raise the bite, even if only by a fraction of a millimeter. When you press or chew on it, all this pressure is transmitted to the inflamed tissues at the root tip and causes tenderness.
What Is "Normal" Tenderness? (Expected Symptoms)
The symptoms we consider "normal," and that we do not want you to worry about, are the following:
§bDuration:§/b This tenderness is usually most noticeable during the first 2–3 days after treatment and should gradually decrease and disappear within a week.
§bType of Pain:§/b It is usually not a "sharp, throbbing" pain but a "dull, aching" one.
§bTrigger:§/b The pain does not usually start on its own (spontaneously). It shows itself only when you press on, touch or try to chew with that tooth.
§bControl:§/b In most cases, the pain can be kept under control with a simple pain reliever (usually containing ibuprofen) prescribed or recommended by your dentist.
If this is the scenario you are experiencing, your body is going through a normal healing process.
Microscope-Assisted Root Canal Treatment and Healing
In delicate procedures such as root canal treatment, we value working while §bseeing the work area under magnification§/b.
One of the important causes of pain that does not go away after treatment is root canals that are hard to see with the naked eye and are "missed" or "incompletely treated."
Contributions of Microscope Support:
§bWorking Under Magnification:§/b Dr. Emrecan Eren works with magnification under a dental microscope.
§bSeeing the Canals:§/b Under the microscope, fine cracks, extra canals and anatomical variations that are hard to see with the naked eye can be seen better.
§bMinimally Invasive Approach:§/b While cleaning infected tissue, we aim to preserve as much healthy tooth structure as possible.
§bCleaning and Filling:§/b The aim is to disinfect the canals and fill them three-dimensionally all the way to the root tip.
§bIn summary:§/b Microscope support helps the canals to be seen in more detail and aims to reduce the risk of the infection returning.
"Not Normal": Which Situations Are Warning Signs? (Call Your Dentist)
If you have any of the following symptoms, this is not "normal healing discomfort," and you should call our clinic right away:
1. If the Character of the Pain Changes:
You have severe, throbbing pain that starts on its own (spontaneously) instead of a mild ache
The pain does not decrease or stop at all despite taking a pain reliever
2. If the Timing of the Pain Changes:
The pain should be decreasing within 3–4 days after treatment, but instead it keeps getting worse
Your pain had gone away, but weeks or months later that tooth began to hurt again
3. If There Is Facial Swelling (Edema):
A swelling that is visible from the outside has formed around the tooth, spreading to your cheek or under your jaw. (This may be a sign that the infection has spread into the bone (acute abscess).)
4. Other Symptoms:
High fever or a general feeling of weakness
Difficulty opening and closing your mouth
A pimple-like swelling (fistula) on the gum over the treated tooth
4 Practical Tips to Support Your Recovery
§bTake Your Medication:§/b If your dentist has prescribed a pain reliever or antibiotic, take it exactly at the times and doses indicated.
§bDon't Use That Side:§/b Until you are told that treatment is complete and the permanent filling or crown has been placed, do not chew hard or sticky foods on the side of that tooth.
§bDon't Stop Your Hygiene:§/b Stopping brushing because the area is tender leads to bacterial buildup and secondary infections.
§bDon't Delay Your Permanent Restoration:§/b Root canal treatment cleans the inside of the tooth. But what really protects the tooth is the permanent filling or crown placed on it.
Conclusion: Transparency and Trust

Mild, temporary tenderness after root canal treatment is a natural part of healing. At our clinic, we aim to make this process as comfortable as possible for you by working with microscopic precision.

However, in line with our "Patient-Centered Communication" principle, listening to your body and contacting us as soon as you notice abnormal "warning signs" (severe pain, swelling) is critically important for the success of this treatment.
§bAbout the Author:§/b This article was written and medically reviewed by §bDr. Emrecan Eren§/b. Our clinic provides care based on evidence-based treatment protocols.

kemik-tozu-greft-nedir.title: What Is Bone Graft Material? Is It Needed for Every Implant?
kemik-tozu-greft-nedir.lead: Insufficient bone, sinus lift and the role of grafting.

b.x: Implant treatment is one of the treatment options used to replace missing teeth. However, during an implant consultation, hearing technical terms such as §b"bone powder," "graft" or "sinus lift"§/b in addition to the word "implant" can understandably cause concern and confusion for patients.
"What is bone powder?", "Why do I need it?", "Will this make the procedure more painful?" are among the first concerns.
In this guide, we will explain what a bone graft is, why it is "sometimes" needed and how the need is assessed (with 3D digital planning).
Why Does an Implant Need Solid Bone?
To understand why a bone graft is needed, we first need to understand how an implant works.

An implant is not simply a "screw" driven into the jawbone. An implant is made of a §b"biocompatible"§/b (body-friendly) material such as titanium. When it is placed in the jawbone, bone cells (osteoblasts) grow toward the implant's specially roughened surface and join with it biologically.
In medicine, this joining process is called §b"osseointegration"§/b. The implant's ability to carry the porcelain crown (the tooth) built on top of it depends on this bonding.

We can compare this to drilling into a solid wall and placing a steel anchor. If the wall is solid (enough bone), the anchor can carry the load. But if the wall is thin, weak or sandy (insufficient bone), the anchor can come loose. For an implant to "hold," it needs a bone wall that is sufficient and healthy in both height and thickness.
Why Is There Insufficient Bone? (Why Is "My" Bone Not Enough?)
So why do some patients have this bone while others do not have enough? There are several common reasons:
Waiting After a Tooth Extraction (a Common Cause):

Our body works on a "use it or lose it" principle. Natural tooth roots keep the bone "active" by transmitting chewing forces to it. When a tooth is extracted, the bone in that area no longer has a function and enters a process of §b"resorption"§/b (shrinking). This loss can be noticeable especially in the first period after extraction. For this reason, waiting too long after an extraction is an important reason that can lead to the need for a graft.
Periodontal (Gum) Diseases:
Long-standing gum inflammation (periodontitis) breaks down not only the gum but also the jawbone that supports the teeth, through infection.
Trauma or Cyst Surgery:
A blow to the area in the past, or surgical removal of a large cyst that formed at the root tip, can lead to loss of bone volume.
Anatomical Limits (Sinus Sagging):

This is especially common for the upper back teeth. Inside the upper jaw there are air spaces called the §b"maxillary sinuses."§/b When the back teeth are extracted, this sinus space "sags" downward due to gravity and takes up the bone height where we would place the implant.
What Exactly Is Bone Graft Material? (Nothing to Be Afraid Of)
Although the term "bone powder" may sound frightening, it is a biocompatible material that is widely used in dentistry.

A bone graft is not a simple "filling material." It acts as a §b"scaffold."§/b Its purpose is to create a "framework" in that area where the body's own bone cells (osteoblasts) can arrive, attach, be nourished and produce new bone. Over time (usually within a few months), your body partially or completely remodels this graft material and forms its own bone tissue in its place.
Types of Graft Material:
The main graft materials used in dentistry are the following:
§bAutograft:§/b Bone taken from the patient's own body (usually the chin or hip). Its advantage is that it is the person's own tissue, but it requires a second surgical site.
§bAllograft:§/b Specially processed, sterile tissue-bank bone taken from another human donor, with all immune cells removed.
§bXenograft:§/b Bone mineral of animal origin (usually bovine). It is a biocompatible material widely used in implant surgery.
§bAlloplast (Synthetic):§/b Synthetic materials produced entirely in a laboratory that imitate bone mineral.
Your dentist (Dr. Eren) will decide on the graft type most suitable for your situation.
What Are the Most Common Graft Procedures?
There are two basic scenarios:
Sinus Lift (Sinus Elevation):

It is used in the "sinus sagging" situation mentioned above. This is a frequently used procedure in the upper back region. The dentist opens a small window in that area, carefully lifts the sinus membrane upward and places the bone graft into the resulting space. In this way, the vertical bone height needed for the implant is gained.
Ridge Augmentation (Bone Thickening / Building):

It is used when the bone has become "thin" after a tooth extraction (like a knife edge). The graft material is placed on the outer surface of the thin bone and sometimes covered with a special protective "membrane." The aim is to add "thickness" to the bone.
The Critical Question: Is a Graft Needed for Every Implant? (Answer: No)
The answer to the main question of this article is §b"No."§/b

Many patients who have recently had a tooth extracted, or who do not have marked bone loss, may have sufficient bone volume for implant placement. In this case, the implant can be placed without needing an additional graft procedure.
So, How Do We Decide Whether It Is Needed?
The decision is based not on guesswork but on §bmeasurements made with imaging§/b.
Before starting treatment, a §b3D Dental Tomography (CBCT)§/b scan is usually taken for implant planning.
Regular 2D panoramic X-rays (OPG) show only the height of the bone, not its thickness.

§b3D tomography (CBCT)§/b, on the other hand, makes it possible to evaluate the bone in three dimensions. On this digital model, the dentist can examine the height and thickness of the area where the implant will be placed, and its distance to the nerve canal and the sinus space.
If, in this digital plan, there is not enough healthy bone of sufficient thickness around the implant, the need for a graft comes up.
How Does It Affect Your Treatment? (Comfort and Time)
These are the questions patients often ask when they learn they need a graft:
1. Pain: Does the graft procedure cause extra pain?

§bAnswer:§/b In most cases, the procedure is done at the same time as the implant surgery and under the same local anesthesia. Tenderness and swelling may occur after the procedure; this is generally similar to what follows an implant operation or tooth extraction. This can be managed with the medication your dentist recommends and a cold compress.
2. Time: Will my treatment take longer?

§bAnswer:§/b This depends on your situation. If the bone deficiency is small, the graft and the implant can be done in the same session. If the bone loss is large (e.g., an advanced sinus lift), the graft is done first, you usually wait a few months (often 4–6 months) for the bone to heal, and then the implant is placed. This waiting period is important so that the bone becomes able to support the implant.
Conclusion: Why Does a Graft Matter "If It Is Needed"?
If your dentist has determined from the 3D tomography that a graft is required, this is generally §ban important prerequisite§/b for the implant to hold in a healthy way.
Ignoring the need for a graft and trying to place an implant in thin or short bone is like "laying a foundation in a swamp."
§bRisk:§/b The implant may not bond with the bone sufficiently (an osseointegration problem).
§bPossible consequences:§/b Loosening of the implant, infection, exposure of the implant surface due to gum recession and, in advanced cases, loss of the implant.

At our clinic in Lüleburgaz, based on 3D digital analyses, we aim to plan in advance the bone support needed for the implant to remain healthy. §bBone grafting is one of the established methods used to provide this support when it is needed.§/b
§bAbout the Author:§/b This article was written and medically reviewed by §bDr. Emrecan Eren§/b. Our clinic provides care based on evidence-based treatment protocols.

kuretaj-derin-temizlik-nedir.title: What Is Curettage (Deep Cleaning)? How Is It Different from Tartar Cleaning?
kuretaj-derin-temizlik-nedir.lead: Treatment of periodontitis, the procedure and what to expect.

b.x: You visited your dentist, perhaps only for a routine check-up or because of bleeding gums. But at the end of the examination, you learned that instead of a "normal tartar cleaning," you need a treatment called §b"Curettage" or "Deep Cleaning."§/b

§bShort answer:§/b Curettage is not just the "next level" of tartar cleaning. The two are meant to treat gum diseases at different stages. Curettage is an important treatment step that aims to reduce the risk of teeth loosening and being lost.
Understanding the Difference: Gingivitis vs. Periodontitis
What separates these two treatments is "where" the disease is.
Stage 1: Gingivitis (Gum Inflammation)
§bWhere the Problem Is:§/b The inflammation is limited to the gums
§bDamage:§/b The gums bleed, swell and turn red. However, there is not yet any loss in the jawbone
§bTreatment:§/b Tartar cleaning (scaling) is sufficient
§bOutcome:§/b With treatment in the early stage, it can usually be reversed
Stage 2 (Advanced): Periodontitis (Gum Disease)
§bWhere the Problem Is:§/b The infection has progressed under the gums, onto the surface of the tooth root and into the jawbone
§b"Periodontal Pocket":§/b Bacteria create deep spaces (3–4 mm or more) between the tooth and the gum
§bThe Culprit:§/b Tartar under the gum and the infected root surface
§bDamage:§/b Bone loss has begun (irreversible)
§bTreatment:§/b Regular cleaning is usually not enough; curettage may be needed
What Exactly Is Curettage? (Step-by-Step Procedure)
Curettage (formally called "Root Surface Planing and Subgingival Curettage") is a treatment that aims to stop the progression of periodontitis.
Step 1: Diagnosis (Measurement Is Essential)
§bPeriodontal Pocket Measurement:§/b We measure the pocket depth around each of your teeth with a special "periodontal probe."
Healthy pocket: 1–3 mm
Periodontitis: 4 mm, 5 mm or deeper
Step 2: Local Anesthesia
Curettage is performed under §blocal anesthesia (an injection)§/b. The aim is that no pain is felt during the procedure thanks to local anesthesia.
Step 3: Root Surface Planing
Once the area is numb, two types of instruments are used:
§bUltrasonic Instruments:§/b Break up large pieces of tartar in the pocket with vibration
§bHand Instruments (Curettes):§/b Go under the gum and carefully scrape off the deposits stuck to the root surface, bacterial plaque and infected tissue
§bGoal:§/b To make the root surface smooth, clean and "biocompatible."
Step 4: Disinfection and Healing
After all the root surfaces have been cleaned, the pockets are rinsed with special antiseptic solutions. The gum, now meeting a "clean" root surface, tends to "reattach" to that surface.
Where Curettage Fits in a "Minimally Invasive" Approach

Curettage is a §bnon-surgical treatment step§/b that lies between "surgical treatment" (flap surgery) and "surface cleaning" (scaling). The aim is, when possible, to bring the disease under control without the need for surgery.
Frequently Asked Questions: Honest Answers
1. "My Teeth Feel Looser After Curettage"
§bHonest Answer:§/b Yes, in the days right after the procedure, such a feeling is temporarily normal.
§bWhy:§/b We have removed the tartar (false support) that was holding the loose teeth together. As the swollen gum heals and tightens, the support of the teeth shows improvement in most cases.
2. "My Gums Have Receded More After Curettage"
§bHonest Answer:§/b Yes, this can be visible and is expected.
§bWhy:§/b The visible "gap" is usually not something caused by curettage; it reflects the bone loss that the disease caused earlier. The swollen gum was hiding it.
3. "I Had a Lot of Pain After the Procedure"
§bHonest Answer:§/b Tenderness lasting 1–2 days after the procedure is normal. It can usually be kept under control with the pain relievers your dentist recommends.
Conclusion: Curettage Is an Important Treatment Step

When periodontitis is diagnosed, curettage is §ban important part of treatment§/b. Periodontitis is a chronic disease. If the source of infection in the deep pockets is not cleaned, the disease can progress:
More bone loss
Increasing tooth mobility
Even teeth without cavities loosening and being lost
In addition, gum diseases are associated with systemic conditions such as §bcardiovascular disease and diabetes§/b. For this reason, oral health should be considered a part of general health.
Curettage is a medical procedure that aims to protect your teeth and improve your gum health.
§bAbout the Author:§/b This article was written and medically reviewed by §bDr. Emrecan Eren§/b. Our clinic provides care based on evidence-based treatment protocols.

mikroskop-destekli-kanal-tedavisi.title: What Is the Dental Microscope Used for in Root Canal Treatment?
mikroskop-destekli-kanal-tedavisi.lead: Magnification, detecting extra canals, and its role in retreatment.

b.x: What Is a Dental Microscope?
A dental microscope is a special optical device used in dentistry that provides §b3x to 30x magnification§/b. In root canal treatment, §b8x-25x magnification§/b is generally used.
What Does the Microscope Change in Root Canal Treatment?

Root canal treatment consists of cleaning the inflamed tissue inside the tooth, shaping and disinfecting the canals, and filling them so that they are sealed. The outcome of the treatment depends on the condition of the tooth, the extent of the inflammation, the canal anatomy, and how the tooth is protected after treatment. At each of these steps, the microscope magnifies and illuminates the working area; it helps the dentist directly see details that are hard to distinguish with the naked eye.
At Which Stages Does the Microscope Help?
1. Detecting Extra Canals
The canal anatomy of teeth is complex, and many teeth have §bextra canals§/b:
§bUpper molars:§/b An MB2 (second mesiobuccal) canal in a significant proportion
§bLower incisors:§/b A second canal in some
§bLower molars:§/b Middle mesial canal variations
A canal left uncleaned can lead to continued inflammation. Magnification makes it easier to see the entrances of these canals.
2. Detecting and Removing Broken Instruments
Although rare, instruments can break during root canal treatment. The microscope:
Helps to see the position of the broken instrument
Can make removal easier in suitable cases
Helps to preserve tooth structure
3. Calcification and Narrow Canals
With age or after trauma, canals can become §bcalcified§/b (narrowed):
The microscope helps to see the canal entrance better
Controlled widening can be performed
Contributes to reducing the risk of perforation
4. Retreatment
The microscope is especially helpful when a previously performed root canal treatment is redone:
Cleaning out the old filling material
Searching for missed canals
Repair of perforations
5. Minimally Invasive Approach
Using a microscope can contribute to §bpreserving tooth structure§/b:
Precise access cavity
Care is taken to preserve healthy tooth structure
In Which Situations Is the Microscope Especially Useful?
Working under magnification makes treatment easier in the following situations:
Root canal retreatment
Calcified canals
Removal of broken instruments
Perforation repair
Apical surgery (root-end resection)
Complex canal anatomy
Conclusion

The dental microscope is a tool that helps the dentist by magnifying and illuminating the working area during root canal treatment. The outcome of the treatment depends on many factors, such as the condition of the tooth, an accurate diagnosis, and protection of the tooth after treatment.
At our clinic, root canal treatments are performed under a dental microscope. After an examination, you can discuss the condition of your tooth with your dentist.

pembe-estetik-gingivektomi.title: What Is Pink Esthetics (Gingivectomy)? The Role of the Gums in a Smile
pembe-estetik-gingivektomi.lead: Gummy smile treatment, laser gingivectomy, and digital smile design.

b.x: When you imagine a beautiful smile, the first thing that comes to mind is probably bright, even, white teeth. That is true, but it is only one part of the equation. No matter how beautiful a painting is, if the frame that displays it is crooked or out of proportion, the painting's beauty is overshadowed.

In dentistry, this "frame" is §byour gums§/b. "Pink esthetics" is an area of esthetic dentistry that examines the harmony and proportion between the teeth (White Esthetics) and the gums that surround them (Pink Esthetics).
What Is "Pink Esthetics"? (The Frame of the Smile)

Pink esthetics is a set of treatment protocols that aim to bring the gums into harmony in terms of shape, color, and level. Healthy gum tissue is pale pink, firm in consistency, and hugs the tooth with a crisp, knife-edge line.
The Most Common Pink Esthetics Concerns:
§b"Gummy Smile":§/b When you smile, noticeably too much gum shows. The teeth look smaller than they are.
§bGum Asymmetry:§/b The gum levels of the teeth on the right and left sides are not aligned.
§bShort-Looking Teeth:§/b The gum has not receded enough from the tooth.
§bGum Pigmentation:§/b Dark spots caused by melanin accumulation.
What Are Gingivectomy and Gingivoplasty?
Although these two terms are often used interchangeably, there is a technical difference between them:
§bGingivectomy (Removal of Gum Tissue):§/b Surgically removing excess gum tissue. Treatment for a "gummy smile."
§bGingivoplasty (Gum Reshaping):§/b Thinning the thickness or form of the gum to give it an ideal, esthetic contour.
§bIn practice:§/b These two procedures are often performed together. While the excess gum is removed, the aim is also to give the area a natural shape.
How Is the Treatment Performed?

This procedure can be performed with a scalpel or with the help of a laser. Which method is suitable is determined by the dentist according to the characteristics of the case. One of the options is §bLaser-Assisted Gingivectomy§/b.
Possible Advantages of Laser Treatment:
§bLess Bleeding:§/b While cutting the tissue, the laser cauterizes (seals by heat) the capillaries, which may reduce bleeding
§bNeed for Sutures:§/b Because the laser seals the tissue edges, sutures may not be needed in many cases
§bHealing:§/b The laser may help reduce the bacterial load in the treatment area
§bComfort:§/b The aim is for there to be less sensitivity after the procedure
§bDuring the Procedure:§/b The procedure is performed under local anesthesia. With local anesthesia, the aim is that no pain is felt during the procedure.
The Critical Question: Will My Gums Grow Back?
One of the reasons the gum may grow back is related to the concept of §b"Biologic Width."§/b
What Is Biologic Width?
For the gum to stay healthy, a §bcertain distance§/b is needed between the gum margin and the point where the jawbone begins.
Where Does the Problem Begin?
If the cause of your "gummy smile" is not only "excess gum" but also "jawbone positioned very close to the gum":
§bUnsuitable Treatment:§/b In this case, if only the gum is cut, the required distance may not be maintained
§bThe Body's Response:§/b The body may regrow the gum to re-establish this distance
The Importance of Planning
§bImaging:§/b When needed, the thickness of the gum and the level of the bone beneath it are evaluated
§bDiagnosis:§/b If the problem is only in the gum, gingivectomy may generally be sufficient
§bChoice of Treatment:§/b If the problem is related to biologic width, a crown lengthening procedure may be needed
Digital Smile Design
At our clinic, pink esthetics planning is carried out with a digital design approach.
§bAnalysis:§/b Photographs of your smile are taken and 3D scans are made
§bDigital Design:§/b The target gum level is planned on smile design software, taking your facial proportions into account
§bExecution:§/b The procedure is carried out based on this digital plan
Conclusion: Adjusting the Frame

Pink esthetics (gingivectomy) is a minimally invasive treatment option aimed at correcting the appearance of a "gummy smile" or gum asymmetry in suitable cases. Results and the healing process may vary from person to person.
The success of this procedure depends on correctly identifying the underlying cause (bone or gum alone).
At our clinic in Lüleburgaz, we focus not only on the teeth but also on the health and harmony of the gums that surround them.

porselen-lamina-kompozit-lamina-karsilas.title: Porcelain Veneers or Composite Veneers (Bonding)? A Decision Guide
porselen-lamina-kompozit-lamina-karsilas.lead: A comparison of the two treatments in terms of esthetics, durability, and number of sessions.

b.x: A small gap (diastema) in your smile, slight crowding, or discoloration that has built up over the years can directly affect your confidence. Modern dentistry offers various options for these esthetic concerns. Two popular options come first among them: §bPorcelain Veneers§/b and §bComposite Veneers (Bonding)§/b.
Questions we often hear from our patients, such as "Which is better for me?", "Which looks more natural?" or "Which lasts longer?", show how important this decision is.

In this guide, we will compare these two esthetic treatments, with their pros and cons, from an impartial point of view. Our aim is to help you make an informed decision about your own smile together with your dentist.
What Are Porcelain Veneers?
Porcelain veneers (also called "laminates") are thin ceramic shells, about as thick as a fingernail (approximately §b0.3 - 0.7 mm§/b), designed to be bonded to the front surface of the teeth.

The process begins with §bdigital smile design§/b. A digital model of your teeth is created with intraoral scanners, and the planned smile is designed. This design is produced in a laboratory either by milling from ceramic blocks (CAD/CAM) or by technicians layering ceramic powders.
Ceramic is a durable material that can provide an appearance close to the translucency and luster of natural tooth enamel.
Porcelain Veneers: What Are the Advantages?
1. Close-to-Natural Esthetics

Ceramic reflects and transmits light in a way similar to natural tooth enamel. This helps achieve a natural, glossy appearance. In restorations of multiple teeth (smile design), a cohesive overall look can be planned.
2. Color Stability (Stain Resistance)

Porcelain is §bmuch less affected§/b than composite by staining foods and drinks such as coffee, tea, cigarettes, or red wine. Thanks to its smooth, non-porous ceramic surface, it tends to keep its color and luster for a long time.
3. Durability

With proper oral care (tooth brushing, flossing) and regular dental checkups, porcelain veneers can be used for §bmany years§/b. Their ceramic structure is generally more resistant to wear than composite materials.
4. Biocompatibility (Gum-Friendly)
Dental ceramics are materials that generally get along well with gum tissue (biocompatible). Their polished surface may help protect gum health by reducing plaque accumulation.
Porcelain Veneers: Disadvantages and Points to Consider
1. Irreversible Procedure (Minimal Tooth Reduction)

For a porcelain veneer to fit the tooth properly and not look bulky, a thin layer, generally between §b0.3 mm and 0.7 mm§/b, needs to be removed (prepared) from the front surface of the tooth. This makes the procedure irreversible. The reduction is planned to preserve healthy tooth structure as much as possible.
2. Process (Multiple Sessions)

Because porcelain veneers require digital design and precise laboratory fabrication, they cannot be completed in one session. Including the impression (digital scan), try-in, and bonding (cementation) stages, it generally takes §b2 or 3 sessions (approximately 7-10 days)§/b.
3. Difficulty of Repair
Although rare, if a porcelain veneer breaks or cracks, it is not as easy to repair as composite. Usually the entire veneer needs to be replaced.
What Are Composite Veneers (Bonding)?

Composite veneering (commonly known as §b"bonding"§/b) is a procedure in which tooth-colored esthetic composite resin material is applied directly to the surface of the tooth, shaped by the dentist, and hardened with a special light.
The whole procedure is done directly in the dental chair, without a laboratory. The anatomical form, color, and luster of the tooth are created through the dentist's manual skill.
Composite Veneers (Bonding): What Are the Advantages?
1. Minimally Invasive (Conservative Dentistry)

In bonding, in most cases no tooth reduction is done, or very little. The tooth surface is roughened with a special solution. This is an approach that preserves healthy tooth structure and is largely reversible.
2. Speed (Single Session)
Even when multiple teeth are treated, the procedure is in most cases completed in §ba single appointment (1-3 hours)§/b. There is no waiting for a laboratory.
3. Easy Repairability
If composite material takes a small knock over time or an edge chips, it can in most cases be repaired or touched up in a short appointment.
Composite Veneers (Bonding): Disadvantages and Points to Consider
1. Risk of Staining

Composite is not a ceramic like porcelain; it is a resin material with microscopic pores. For this reason, over time it can §bstain§/b under the effect of coloring substances such as coffee, tea, and cigarettes, and lose its luster.
2. Durability
It is generally less resistant to wear and fracture than porcelain veneers. It may need to be renewed over time or extensively repolished.
3. Esthetic Limitations

The translucency and luster of composite material may not always fully capture the §b"glass-like"§/b look that porcelain offers. This difference can be more noticeable, especially when multiple teeth are involved.
Quick Comparison: Porcelain Veneers vs. Composite Veneers

rows: Easier (in most cases in a single session)

b.x: In Which Situation Might Each Be Considered?
There is no single right option for everyone; the decision is made together with the dentist, based on examination findings and personal expectations.
Porcelain veneers may be considered in the following situations:
If you want a cohesive design and color change across §bmultiple teeth§/b (e.g., 6-8 teeth) in your smile
If your teeth have §badvanced discoloration§/b (e.g., tetracycline staining) that composite would not cover
If you are looking for a long-term, stain-resistant option
If a process of a few sessions (2-3 sessions) suits your schedule
Composite veneers (bonding) may be considered in the following situations:
If a §bminimally invasive§/b (conservative) approach is your first priority and you do not want your teeth touched at all
If you only want to fix §bsmall esthetic problems on one or two teeth§/b (a small chip, closing a gap)
If you are looking for a §bquick, single-session§/b solution (e.g., if you have a wedding or graduation coming up)
Especially in §byoung patients§/b, bonding is often considered first in order to preserve tooth structure
Conclusion: An Informed Decision
Both porcelain veneers and composite bonding are options used in esthetic dentistry. One is a more §bdurable and stain-resistant§/b approach; the other is a §bquicker and tooth-preserving§/b one.

At our clinic in Lüleburgaz, before deciding on treatment, an examination and, when needed, §bdigital smile design§/b are carried out. Your expectations are listened to, the options are explained with their advantages and disadvantages, and the decision is made together.

seffaf-plak-dis-teli-karsilastirma.title: Clear Aligners or Traditional Braces? Which Is Right for You?
seffaf-plak-dis-teli-karsilastirma.lead: A comparison in terms of esthetics, comfort, and hygiene.

b.x: After deciding on orthodontic treatment, a second question often comes up: §b"How will I reach this goal? With braces or with clear aligners?"§/b
This guide is an §binformational text§/b prepared to help you evaluate the two options in terms of your lifestyle, your esthetic expectations, and the current condition of your teeth.
What Are Traditional Braces?
Traditional orthodontics, that is, "brackets and wires," is a system that has been used for many years and is widely applied.
Advantages of Traditional Braces:
§bStrength and Scope:§/b They can also be used in complex cases that require advanced rotation of teeth or that involve serious bite problems.
§bContinuous Effect:§/b The wires are fixed and cannot be removed by the patient. This reduces reliance on the patient's compliance with wear.
Disadvantages of Traditional Braces:
§bEsthetic Concern:§/b Especially for adult patients, the visibility of metal wires is a source of concern in social and professional life.
§bComfort Issues:§/b Metal brackets and wire ends can cause sores on the insides of the cheeks and lips.
§bDifficult Hygiene:§/b Food debris can easily build up around the brackets. Brushing the teeth is harder.
§bDietary Restrictions:§/b Avoiding hard, sticky, and acidic foods is recommended.
What Is Clear Aligner Treatment?
Clear aligner treatment is a digital orthodontic method that, instead of metal wires, uses a series of custom-made, barely noticeable, clear plastic "aligners" to straighten teeth.
How Does It Work?
§b3D Digital Scan:§/b With our intraoral 3D scanners, we create a digital twin of your teeth.
§bDigital Treatment Planning:§/b The movements of the teeth are planned step by step in a digital environment.
§b3D Production:§/b A pair of "clear aligners" is produced for each step on 3D printers.
§bTreatment:§/b The patient wears each aligner 22 hours a day. Each new aligner moves the teeth to the next step in the digital plan.
Advantages of Clear Aligner Treatment:
§bEsthetics:§/b The aligners are transparent and barely noticeable in the mouth.
§bComfort:§/b There is no risk of the sores and aphthae associated with metal brackets.
§bHygiene:§/b The aligners are removable; you can brush your teeth more easily.
§bEating:§/b Because the aligners are taken out while eating, there are fewer food restrictions.
§bSeeing the Plan:§/b Before starting treatment, you can see the planned tooth movements on a 3D simulation.
Disadvantages of Clear Aligner Treatment:
§bPatient Compliance Is Required:§/b The aligners must be worn for the period recommended by the dentist (generally 20-22 hours a day). Discipline is important.
§bScope:§/b Not every case may be suitable for clear aligner treatment; suitability is determined by examination.
Quick Comparison Table
Which Should You Choose?
The decision is made together with your dentist, based on examination findings and your personal expectations.
Traditional braces may be considered in the following situations:
Very complex cases or cases that require surgery
Situations where compliance with wearing aligners may be difficult (e.g., young age)
Clear aligner treatment may be considered in the following situations:
Adults and working professionals
Those who prioritize esthetics and comfort
Those with high hygiene expectations
Disciplined and motivated patients
Conclusion
Both methods have their own advantages and limitations. In suitable cases, digital planning and clear aligners offer additional options in terms of esthetics and comfort.
At our clinic in Lüleburgaz, we make the treatment decision together with you. We listen to you, take your 3D scan, and show you the advantages of both options on a "digital simulation."

sut-disleri-neden-onemli.title: Why Are Baby Teeth Important? The Scientific Answer to the "They'll Fall Out Anyway" Myth
sut-disleri-neden-onemli.lead: The vital importance of baby teeth for permanent tooth health, jaw development, and speech.

b.x: As a parent, you always want the best for your child's health. But when it comes to dental health, you run into one of the most common and most dangerous myths going around: §b"Baby teeth will fall out anyway, so there is no need to treat cavities."§/b
Although this thought seems like an innocent delay, from the standpoint of modern dentistry it is §ba misconception that may put your child's long-term oral and jaw health at risk.§/b
The 4 Vital Roles of Baby Teeth
The first fact that dismantles the "they'll fall out anyway" myth is the "vital" roles that baby teeth take on during that "temporary" period of 6-12 years.
Role 1 (The Most Important): A "Natural Space Holder" for Permanent Teeth
The primary role of baby teeth is to §b"hold the space"§/b for the permanent tooth that will come in from beneath.
§bNatural Guidance:§/b Beneath the root of every baby tooth, a permanent tooth bud waits like a "seed"
§bHow the Process Works:§/b When it is time for the permanent tooth to erupt, it "dissolves" the roots of the baby tooth. Once its roots dissolve, the baby tooth becomes loose and falls out
§bResult:§/b The permanent tooth settles into exactly that space
Role 2: Jaw Development and Nutrition
The chewing function is the main "growth signal" that triggers the healthy growth of your child's facial and jaw bones.
§bCavities and Pain:§/b A child in pain stops chewing effectively. Chewing on one side creates asymmetry in the jaw joint
§bMalnutrition:§/b A child who avoids hard foods because of pain tends to eat only soft, carbohydrate-heavy foods
Role 3: Speech Development (Phonetics)
During the critical age of 2-5 when your child learns to speak, the tongue's ability to produce the right sounds depends on the presence of the front baby teeth.
§bCritical Sounds:§/b Sounds such as "S", "Sh", "Z", "F", "V", "T" are produced by the tongue touching the front teeth
§bEarly Loss:§/b Front baby teeth lost early because of decay can set the stage for a lisp and lasting speech disorders
Role 4: Psychological and Social Development

Especially between the ages of 3-6, when social development begins, the esthetics of a smile directly affect a child's self-confidence. Front teeth that look "black" or "broken" because of decay can make a child shy away from smiling and withdraw socially.
How Can Baby Tooth Decay Affect the Permanent Tooth?
This is the most important fact that refutes the "they'll fall out anyway" myth: §bA baby tooth cavity is not a simple "hole"; it is "an infectious disease."§/b
The Chain of Infection:
Bacteria pass through the enamel of the baby tooth and reach the dentin
If left untreated, they descend to the nerve (pulp)
When the nerve of the baby tooth becomes infected, the infection spreads out through the tip of the root
It spreads into the jawbone and forms an "abscess"
§bRight beneath that abscess:§/b is the seed of the developing permanent tooth
Result: "Turner Tooth" (Turner's Hypoplasia)
A chronic infection coming from a baby tooth can adversely affect the development of the enamel of the permanent tooth that is forming right beneath it, during its formation stage.
When the permanent tooth erupts into the mouth years later, it comes in with §b"yellow or brown spots," "pits," or "shape defects"§/b on it.

§bImportant:§/b These spots do not go away with brushing; they show that the enamel of the tooth was affected during its formation stage. A simple filling not done on the baby tooth in time may lead to a need for more extensive treatment on the permanent tooth later on.
The Domino Effect: "One Tooth Is Extracted, the Whole Jaw Shifts"
Let's say the decay progressed a great deal and a baby molar was extracted. This situation can be the start of a second problem.
What Happens When the "Space Holder" Is Lost?
§bThe 6-Year Molar Moves Forward:§/b Right behind the baby molar, the "first permanent molar" erupts. This tooth is the "keystone" of the mouth
§bThe Space Closes:§/b Seeing that the baby tooth in front of it has been extracted, the 6-year molar begins to drift toward that gap
§bThe Permanent Tooth Stays Impacted:§/b Years later, the "permanent premolar" that should come in beneath the extracted baby molar cannot find room for itself
§bPossible Outcome:§/b A baby tooth that was not treated early on because "it'll fall out anyway" and was extracted instead may lead to a need for orthodontic treatment (braces) in later years.
Our Clinic's Approach: Prevention First
"Evidence-Based" Diagnosis
Not every brown spot on a tooth means an "active cavity." Sometimes it may be an "arrested cavity" or "staining." At our clinic, we do not place any unnecessary fillings.
"Preventive Dentistry" (Our Philosophy)
Our aim is not so much to treat cavities as to keep cavities from forming in the first place:
§bFissure Sealant:§/b As soon as the permanent molars erupt, we cover their grooved surfaces with a protective coating
§bFluoride Application:§/b Professional fluoride varnish applications that strengthen tooth enamel
Treatment (If Needed)

If a cavity has formed, we place a filling or perform root canal treatment on the baby tooth using biocompatible materials to keep that infection from harming the permanent tooth. §bThe goal is to protect the permanent tooth coming in from beneath.§/b
Conclusion: Baby Teeth Are the Foundation of the Future
The idea that "baby teeth will fall out anyway" is a dangerous myth with no scientific basis, one that modern dentistry rejects entirely.
Baby teeth are the guide for permanent teeth, the engine of jaw development, the trainer of speech, and a part of your child's self-confidence.
Regular dental checkups from the moment your child's first tooth erupts (or at the latest from age 1) are an important step in protecting your child's oral health.

zirkonyum-kaplama-renk-secimi.title: How to Choose the Color of Zirconia Crowns: 5 Tips for a Natural Look
zirkonyum-kaplama-renk-secimi.lead: The shade guide, matching natural teeth, and the role of digital design.

b.x: Zirconia crowns are among the restorations commonly used in dentistry for their durability and esthetic properties. However, a concern that patients often voice when deciding on this treatment is this: §b"What if my crowns look 'fake'?"§/b

Problems created by the metal-supported porcelain used in the past, such as opacity (a flat, matte look) and a "dark gum line," have stayed in people's memories. Metal-free zirconia and digital dentistry methods can help reduce these problems.
The right shade is not always the whitest shade; it is the shade that suits your face and skin tone and aims for a natural look.
The Secret of Natural Teeth: Color Is Not Just "Whiteness"

The color of a natural tooth is not made up of a single "white" tone. On the contrary, it has an incredibly complex structure. Even the §bshade guides§/b we use in dentistry to standardize colors can only simplify this complexity.
The color of a natural tooth is made up of 3 main components:
§bHue (Main Color Tone):§/b The main color character of the tooth. It is generally in yellowish-reddish (group A), yellowish (group B), grayish (group C), or grayish-reddish (group D) tones.
§bChroma (Saturation):§/b Indicates how "intense" that main color tone is (e.g., A1, A2, A3; A1 is the lightest, A3 the most intense yellowish-red).
§bValue (Brightness):§/b Shows how light or dark the tooth is, that is, how much light it reflects.

Patients usually focus only on §b"Value" (brightness)§/b and ask for the whitest shades such as "B1" or "BL1" (Bleach). Yet the real factors that create naturalness are the balance of Hue, Chroma, and the "Translucency" (light transmission) we will discuss shortly.
5 Tips for a Natural Look
In choosing a shade, 5 basic principles that evaluate these three components together with your personal features can serve as a guide:
1. Are the Whitest Shades (Bleach) Right for Everyone? (Skin Tone & Eye Harmony)
The "whitest" shades that are often requested, that is, the "Bleach" (BL) shades, may not always be a suitable option. Our first rule in shade selection is §bharmony§/b.
The Whites-of-the-Eyes (Sclera) Rule:

A practical guide is the white of your eyes (the sclera). §bYour new teeth should not be whiter than the whites of your eyes.§/b If the teeth are brighter than the whites of the eyes, all attention is drawn to the teeth and this creates an "artificial" look.
Matching Skin Tone:

On a patient with darker skin, a very bright, white (BL1) shade may not look natural; instead, a bright shade with a warmer undertone (such as A1 or B1) may look more harmonious. People with fair skin, on the other hand, can carry cooler and brighter shades better.
Remember, the goal is not to have "white teeth" but to have §b"a natural, healthy-looking smile."§/b
2. Translucency: The Technical Key to Naturalness

Your natural teeth are not opaque (as if painted). They absorb and reflect light to a certain degree. In particular, the biting edges of the teeth (incisal edges) have a more translucent (transparent) structure. This slight translucency adds §b"vitality" and "depth"§/b to the tooth.
Multi-Layer Zirconia:

§b"Multi-layer"§/b zirconia blocks are manufactured to imitate this transition. While the gum-side portion of these blocks is more opaque and saturated in color, the color lightens and translucency increases toward the biting edges.
The "opaque and matte" look that can be seen with metal-supported porcelain can be noticeably reduced with this type of material.
3. Digital Design: Evaluating the Result in Advance
Shade selection can be supported by the §b"digital design"§/b process.
§b3D Scan:§/b First, we take a digital model of your teeth with our intraoral 3D scanners.
§bDigital Smile Design (DSD):§/b On this model, we plan your new smile using "Digital Smile Design" software.
§bDigital Shade Simulation:§/b On this design, we apply the selected shade (e.g., A1 or BL2) and, before moving on to fabrication, simulate on screen approximately how the result will look (Mock-up).

This approach helps expectations to be discussed before treatment and makes the result more predictable. The simulation is a preview; the actual result may differ depending on individual characteristics.
4. The Shade of the Surrounding Teeth (Single Tooth vs. Full Smile Design)
Shade selection changes entirely depending on how many teeth will be treated:
Scenario 1: Single-Tooth Zirconia Crown
This is a technically demanding restoration. The aim is for the crown to be indistinguishable from the neighboring natural tooth.

In this case, the dentist must analyze not only the main shade (Hue, Chroma, Value) but also all the characteristic details on the neighboring tooth, such as fine "white spots," "mamelons" (the bumps on the tooth's edge), or "translucency," and communicate them to the laboratory.
Scenario 2: Full Smile Design (6-10 Teeth)
Here we have more freedom. Because we will not be comparing with neighboring teeth, we can determine a new main shade according to skin tone and the whites-of-the-eyes rule (Tip 1).
Even so, it is important for overall esthetics not to create too great a "shade difference" with the color of the natural teeth in the lower jaw.
5. Dentist-Technician Communication and Your Final Approval (Try-In)
Materials and technology alone are not enough. Shade selection is a §bcollaboration§/b between the dentist, the patient, and the dental technician.
The Dentist's Role:

Your dentist analyzes all of these technical details (the shade guide, translucency, special characteristics). They take digital photographs and present this information to the ceramist at the laboratory as a detailed "prescription."
The Try-In Appointment:

After your crowns arrive from the laboratory, they are generally not permanently bonded right away. A §b"try-in"§/b appointment is held. In this appointment, the teeth are placed in your mouth temporarily.
Your Approval:

At this stage, we ask you to look in the mirror and examine them under different lights (daylight, clinic light). Your views on the color, shape, and position are taken; adjustments are made if needed.
Your approval is the last step before bonding.
Conclusion: A Natural Color Is a Color That Goes Unnoticed

In short, choosing the right shade for a zirconia crown is not just choosing "the whitest." A natural result means choosing a shade that harmonizes with your skin tone, is not brighter than the whites of your eyes, has natural translucency, and is designed specifically for you digitally.
§bRemember:§/b The goal of an esthetic restoration is not for people to say "What nice crowns you have," but §b"What a nice smile you have"§/b, that is, for it to go unnoticed.
At our clinic in Lüleburgaz, we focus not just on the color of a single tooth but on how that tooth harmonizes with your smile, your face, and your health.

zirkonyum-porselen-kopru-karsilastirma.title: Zirconia Bridge or Porcelain Bridge? Which Material Is Right for You?
zirkonyum-porselen-kopru-karsilastirma.lead: A comparison of esthetics, durability, and biocompatibility.

b.x: Replacing a missing tooth (bridge treatment) is not only an esthetic concern but also an important step in protecting your chewing function and oral health. Once you decide on treatment, an important question comes up: §b"What material should my bridge be made of?"§/b
Is it the "porcelain bridge" you have heard about for years, or the "zirconia bridge" commonly used today?
"Porcelain Bridge": Porcelain-Fused-to-Metal (PFM)
When our patients say "porcelain bridge," they generally mean the traditional type of bridge that has been used for decades, whose technical name is §b"Porcelain-Fused-to-Metal" (PFM)§/b.
How Does It Work?
PFM bridges consist of two layers:
§bInner Structure (Substructure):§/b A gray metal alloy framework
§bOuter Structure (Superstructure):§/b Tooth-colored porcelain fired onto the metal framework
Advantages of PFM:
§bDurability:§/b Resistant to chewing forces thanks to its metal substructure
§bLong History of Use:§/b A method that has been widely used for many years
Disadvantages of PFM:
1. More Opaque Esthetics
The metal substructure beneath blocks the passage of light. For this reason, in some cases a more matte and opaque appearance may result.
2. The "Gray Gum Line" Problem
A complaint that can be seen over time with PFM bridges is a purple-gray line forming at the gum margin. The possible causes are as follows:
§bMetal Show-Through:§/b The gray shadow of the metal beneath shows through thin gum tissue
§bGum Recession:§/b If the gum recedes over time, the "metal margin" of the bridge beneath becomes visible
§bMetal Oxidation:§/b Metal alloys can corrode in saliva, which may cause "tattoo"-like discoloration of the gum
3. Biocompatibility Concerns
Although rare, metal alloys can cause allergic reactions, gum irritation, or a metallic taste in the mouth in some patients.
What Is a Zirconia Bridge?
Zirconia (zirconium dioxide) is a ceramic material with high strength. It is also used in the medical field (for example, in some joint prostheses).
Types of Zirconia
§bMonolithic Zirconia:§/b Fabricated from a single solid zirconia block. It shows high resistance to fracture; it is often preferred for bridges on the back molars.
§bMulti-Layer Zirconia:§/b Fabricated in layers, similar to a natural tooth. Translucency increases toward the biting edges.
Advantages of a Zirconia Bridge
1. Biocompatibility
§bContains No Metal:§/b May be a suitable option for patients with metal allergy
§bGray Gum Line:§/b Because there is no metal beneath, the gray line caused by metal does not form
2. Esthetics
§bTranslucency:§/b The semi-transparent structure of zirconia helps achieve an appearance close to the natural tooth
§bNo Metal Shadow:§/b Does not cast a metal-related gray shadow on the gum
3. Durability
Zirconia is more durable than traditional porcelain. Its resistance to chewing forces is comparable to that of PFMs with a metal substructure.
4. Digital Fabrication
Zirconia is not made by hand. It is fabricated §bdigitally (CAD/CAM)§/b:
§b3D Scan (CAD):§/b We take a digital impression of your mouth
§bDigital Design:§/b Your bridge is designed on the computer
§bMachine Fabrication (CAM):§/b Your bridge is produced by milling in a milling machine

§bResult:§/b Digital fabrication helps make the "marginal fit" where the bridge meets the tooth precise. A good marginal fit and regular oral care contribute to reducing the risk of decay in the abutment teeth.
Quick Comparison Table

rows: Limited in people with metal allergy

b.x: Conclusion
The "porcelain bridge" (PFM) is a sturdy option that has been used for many years. Zirconia, on the other hand, may offer additional advantages in terms of §bbiocompatibility and esthetics§/b.

At the Dr. Emrecan Eren Polyclinic, we often consider §bzirconia bridges§/b in suitable cases because they can meet these three expectations together. The final decision is made together with the patient after the examination.

kanita-dayali-dis-hekimligi.title: What Is Evidence-Based Dentistry?
kanita-dayali-dis-hekimligi.lead: Considering scientific evidence, clinical experience, and patient preferences together.

b.x: As a patient, when making a decision about your health, you are quite likely to find yourself in the middle of a barrage of information. On one side are the "miraculous" and "fast" esthetic trends you see on the internet and social media; on the other are hearsay "fears" with no scientific basis ("Fluoride is poison", "Scaling scratches the enamel").
One of the approaches meant to serve as a guide through this tangle of information is §b"Evidence-Based Dentistry" (EBD)§/b.
What Is "Evidence-Based Dentistry"?

"Evidence-Based Medicine" is the philosophy that a clinician should make treatment decisions not on subjective assumptions such as "that's how I was taught" or "this new device is very popular," but on §b"scientific evidence."§/b
The 3 Main Pillars:
1. Scientific Evidence
Research sources such as systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and clinical studies. These sources are drawn upon when comparing treatment options.
2. Clinical Experience
Scientific evidence provides "general" knowledge. The dentist's clinical experience helps assess how to apply this knowledge to your case.
3. Patient Preferences
An option that is generally recommended may not always be the most suitable one for your lifestyle or esthetic expectations.
The Trap of "Fashion" vs. the Fear of "Myth"
The evidence-based approach aims to keep a balance in two directions:
1. Avoiding Overtreatment
❌ Common trend: "Grinding down all the teeth for esthetics"

§b✅ Evidence-based approach:§/b Preserving healthy tooth structure is important. In suitable cases, more conservative options such as teeth whitening, clear aligners, or composite bonding may be considered first.
❌ Common trend: "Activated charcoal toothpastes"
§b✅ Evidence-based approach:§/b There are concerns that such toothpastes may be abrasive and can damage enamel; regular use is not recommended.
2. Not Delaying Necessary Treatment Because of Misconceptions
❌ Misconception: "Scaling scratched my teeth"

§b✅ Evidence-based approach:§/b When performed correctly, ultrasonic cleaning does not damage enamel. The "gaps" noticed after cleaning are mostly disease-related gum and bone loss that the tartar had previously been covering.
❌ Misconception: "Fluoride is poison"

§b✅ Evidence-based approach:§/b Professional topical fluoride applied at the appropriate dose is one of the established methods that help reduce the risk of decay. The risk comes from an excessive dose rather than from fluoride itself.
What the Evidence-Based Approach Looks Like in Practice
1. Imaging: 3D Tomography
When needed (for example, in implant planning), 3D tomography helps in the three-dimensional evaluation of the bone structure and anatomical structures such as the nerve canal.
2. Magnification: Microscope
Using magnification in root canal treatment can help in noticing additional canals that may be hard to see with the naked eye.
3. Minimally Invasive Approach
In suitable cases, in order to preserve healthy tooth structure, more conservative options such as a composite filling that bonds to the tooth may be considered instead of a crown.
4. Choice of Material
Materials such as porcelain-fused-to-metal and zirconia have different properties in terms of esthetics and tissue compatibility. The choice of material is made according to the case.
5. Bruxism Treatment
A night guard is a common option in bruxism.
What Does This Mean for You as a Patient?
Treatment Based on Need
Treatment recommendations aim to be based on your examination findings, not on popular trends.
Planned Treatment
When needed, treatment is planned using tools such as digital imaging and magnification.
You Become a Partner in Treatment
The reasons for the treatment and the options are explained to you clearly. You make the decision in an informed way.
Conclusion
Evidence-based dentistry is an approach that considers current scientific knowledge, the dentist's clinical experience, and the patient's preferences together.
In line with this approach, our aim is to evaluate with you minimally invasive treatment options that take the whole of oral and dental health into account.
